title: Networking and the cloud
intro: Every deploy in this course travels over a network, and most production systems run in someone else's data center. Part 3 follows one request in the order things happen to it. Day 10 covers names, addresses and ports, Day 11 the HTTP conversation and the servers in the middle, and Day 12 the rented cloud around it all. Days 13 and 14 make that cloud real: an AWS account on the Free plan, the CLI, IAM, S3 and a small server of your own. They cost a few cents of credits. Without an account, every AWS command also runs against a local emulator.

lessons.title: How computers find each other: IP, ports and DNS
lessons.goal: By the end you can read an IP address and a CIDR block, explain how a name becomes an address, and tell from an error message which step of a connection failed.

guess.q: Which network holds more addresses: 10.0.0.0/16 or 10.0.0.0/24?
options: 10.0.0.0/24, because 24 is bigger than 16
10.0.0.0/16, with 65,536 addresses
They hold the same number of addresses
It depends on the router's settings
guess.why: The number after the slash counts the fixed bits. More fixed bits leave fewer free ones, so /16 has 65,536 addresses and /24 only 256.

terms.plain: A number that identifies one network interface, such as 192.168.1.23 or 127.0.0.1.
An address from a range that many networks reuse inside (10.x, 172.16 to 172.31, 192.168.x) and that the internet never routes.
A way to write a block of addresses: 10.0.1.0/24 means the first 24 bits are fixed, which leaves 256 addresses.
Network address translation: a router swaps private addresses for its own public address on the way out, and back on the way in.
A number from 0 to 65535 that picks which program on a machine receives the traffic.
A transport protocol that opens a connection with a handshake and delivers bytes in order, resending anything lost.
A server that answers 'what is the address of this name?' by asking other DNS servers and caching the answers.
Time to live: how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached and reused before someone must ask again.

sections.h: IP addresses: where a machine lives
sections.body:
Every request starts with an address. An IP address identifies one network interface: the hardware or software that connects a machine to a network. It does the job a street address does for a building.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255, such as `192.168.1.23`. Each number is one byte (8 bits), which is why it stops at 255. The 32 bits give about 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough for every device on earth. IPv6 fixes this with 128-bit addresses written in hex, such as `2001:db8::1`. You will see IPv6 in tool output, and it works the same way. This course mostly uses IPv4 because the numbers are easier to read.

Your laptop has several addresses at once:

- One on Wi-Fi, handed out by your home router.
- `127.0.0.1`, the loopback address, which always means "this machine".
- More inside Docker Desktop's Linux VM, one per Docker network.

The 4.3 billion limit is why some addresses are private. These ranges are reused inside millions of homes, offices and cloud networks, and routers on the internet never forward them. The number after each slash is explained in the CIDR section below:

- `10.0.0.0/8`: every address that starts with 10.
- `172.16.0.0/12`: from 172.16 to 172.31.
- `192.168.0.0/16`: every address that starts with 192.168.

Every other normal address is public and unique on the whole internet. Your laptop almost certainly has a private one, such as `192.168.1.23`. If you see an address starting with `100.64` to `100.127` on a phone hotspot or a VPN, that is a special shared range for providers, not a public address.

sections.h: NAT and the way out of your house
sections.body:
So how does a laptop with a private address reach GitHub? Through your home router, using NAT (network address translation). The router has one public address from your internet provider. Data travels in packets: small chunks, each labelled with a source and a destination address. When your laptop sends a packet out, the router does three things:

1. It replaces your private source address with its public one.
2. It remembers the swap, so it knows the reply belongs to your laptop.
3. When the reply comes back, it swaps the address back and passes the reply to you.

Everyone in your home shares that one public address. That is why a website sees your router's address, never your laptop's. It also explains why nobody outside can start a connection to your laptop: the router has no record for traffic it never saw go out.

Your laptop knows to send those packets to the router because of its route table. Every machine has one: a short list of rules that says where to send traffic for each block of addresses. A laptop usually has two kinds of rule. Addresses on its own network go straight to the destination. Everything else goes to the default gateway, which is your router. When two rules match, the more specific one wins: the one that covers fewer addresses.

Your router has a route table of its own, whose default gateway is at your internet provider. Each router on the way reads the destination address and passes the packet one hop closer. `traceroute`, near the end of this lesson, lists those hops.

Day 12 brings the same ideas back in a cloud network, with an internet gateway, a NAT gateway and route tables that you write yourself.

sections.h: CIDR: reading /24 and /16
sections.body:
Route tables, firewall rules and cloud networks all talk about blocks of addresses, not single ones. A block is written in CIDR notation (Classless Inter-Domain Routing): an address, a slash and a number. The number says how many bits at the start are fixed. Those fixed bits name the network. The remaining bits number the machines inside it. Each of the four numbers is 8 bits, so `/24` fixes the first three numbers and leaves the last one free.

An IPv4 address has 32 bits, so a block holds 2 to the power of (32 minus N) addresses:

- `/32`: 1 address, a single machine.
- `/24`: 256 addresses, such as `10.0.1.0` to `10.0.1.255`.
- `/16`: 65,536 addresses, such as `10.0.0.0` to `10.0.255.255`.
- `/8`: 16,777,216 addresses, everything that starts with `10.`.

The direction feels backwards at first: a bigger number after the slash means a smaller network. Each extra fixed bit halves the block, so a `/25` is half a `/24`, 128 addresses.

You will also meet an older way to write the same thing, the subnet mask. `255.255.255.0` means /24 and `255.255.0.0` means /16. On a Mac, `ifconfig` prints the mask in hex, and `0xffffff00` is /24.

You do not need binary drills. Python's `ipaddress` module checks your math. `python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; print(i.ip_network('10.0.0.0/16').num_addresses)"` prints `65536`.

sections.h: Ports, and how TCP and UDP deliver
sections.body:
An IP address gets traffic to the right machine. A port picks the right program on that machine, like an apartment number in a building. A port is a number from 0 to 65535. Servers listen on well-known ports, agreed numbers that tell a client where to knock. A URL like `https://github.com` names no port, so your browser uses 443. The common ones:

- 22: SSH
- 53: DNS
- 80: HTTP
- 443: HTTPS
- 5432: PostgreSQL
- 6379: Redis

The client uses a port too, picked at random from a high range for each connection. It is called an ephemeral port. Four values define one connection: source address, source port, destination address and destination port. That is how one laptop keeps 50 browser tabs apart. Your router's NAT uses the same four values to tell your laptop's connections from your phone's, and it may change the source port too. An address together with a port is called a socket.

Two transport protocols carry the data. TCP is like registered mail with receipts. Before any data moves, the client and server do a three-step handshake:

1. The client sends SYN: "I want to talk."
2. The server answers SYN-ACK: "Fine, I hear you."
3. The client sends ACK, and the connection is open.

After that, TCP numbers every byte, and the receiver acknowledges what has arrived. The sender resends anything not acknowledged in time, and the receiver puts the bytes back in order. HTTP, SSH and database connections use TCP.

UDP is a postcard: no handshake and no guarantee. It is lighter, so it suits small questions and live media. DNS uses UDP on port 53 for most queries. HTTP/3 runs over UDP too, through a protocol called QUIC, and Day 11 comes back to that.

sections.h: Loopback, 0.0.0.0 and why containers bind to 0.0.0.0
sections.body:
A server program binds to an address and a port, then listens there. The address it binds to decides who can reach it. People get this wrong more than anything else on this page:

- Binding to `127.0.0.1` accepts connections from the same machine only. Loopback traffic never leaves the machine.
- Binding to `0.0.0.0` means "listen on every address this machine has": Wi-Fi, loopback and any others alike.

Development servers often choose `127.0.0.1` by default, so nobody else on your Wi-Fi can reach a half-finished app. Flask's built-in server does this, which matters in a moment.

`0.0.0.0` is a wildcard for listening, and you never connect to it. The tools show the difference. On Linux, `ss -tlnp` shows one server on `127.0.0.1:9101` and another on `0.0.0.0:9102`. On a Mac, `lsof` shows the second one as `*:9102`, where the star means every address.

A container gets its own network stack with its own loopback, like a tiny separate machine (Day 17 covers containers properly). Publishing a port with `-p 8000:8000` tells Docker to pass connections from port 8000 on your Mac to port 8000 in the container. Docker delivers them to the container's network address, not to its loopback. So an app inside the container that binds to `127.0.0.1` never receives them. curl then prints something like `Empty reply from server` or `Connection reset by peer`. The fix is to bind to `0.0.0.0` inside the container. That is why `app.py` ends with `host="0.0.0.0"`, which overrides Flask's default.

Publishing also opens the port wider than you might expect. `-p 8000:8000` publishes the port on every address of your Mac, so other machines on your Wi-Fi may reach it. Docker's own docs call port publishing "insecure by default". Write `-p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000` when only your laptop should connect.

sections.h: DNS: from names to addresses
sections.body:
People remember names, and machines connect to addresses. DNS, the Domain Name System, turns one into the other. It is a phone book spread over many thousands of servers, with caches everywhere. No single server could hold every name, so the work is split along the dots in a name, and each level only knows who runs the level below it. When your app looks up `github.com`, the question travels this chain:

1. The stub resolver, a small part of your operating system, checks `/etc/hosts` and its own cache.
2. If it has no answer, it asks a recursive resolver: your router, your internet provider, or a public one such as `1.1.1.1`.
3. If that resolver has nothing cached, it asks a root server, which says "ask the servers for .com".
4. A .com server, called a TLD (top-level domain) server, says "ask github.com's own name servers".
5. The authoritative server for github.com gives the real answer.
6. The answer flows back, and each layer caches it.

Your laptop learned which recursive resolver to use from the router, when it got its own address. Every recursive resolver ships with the root servers' addresses, so it always has a place to start.

Each answer is a record, and these are the types you will meet:

- A: name to IPv4 address.
- AAAA: name to IPv6 address.
- CNAME: this name is an alias, so look up that other name instead.
- MX: which servers accept email for the domain.
- TXT: free text, used to prove you own a domain and for email policy.
- NS: which servers are authoritative for the domain.

Every record has a TTL in seconds: how long anyone may cache it. People say a DNS change takes time to "propagate". What really happens is that old answers sit in caches until their TTL runs out. So after a change, one colleague reaches the new server while another still reaches the old one. Teams lower the TTL a day before a planned move.

`/etc/hosts` is a local file that beats DNS, for your machine only. Watch out with `dig`, though: it asks DNS servers directly and ignores `/etc/hosts`, while your apps and `ping` read that file first. If `dig` and your app disagree about a name, look in `/etc/hosts`.

sections.h: Refused, timed out or unresolved: reading the error
sections.body:
When a connection fails, the exact error tells you which step broke. Four errors cover most cases:

- Could not resolve host, or "Name or service not known": DNS failed. No packet went to the server at all.
- Connection refused: the machine answered your SYN with a reset, because nothing listens on that port. The app is down, on another port, or bound to `127.0.0.1`.
- Timed out: nothing answered. A firewall dropped the packets, or the address is wrong or unreachable.
- Connection reset, or an empty reply: something accepted the connection and then closed it. Proxies and Docker's port forwarder do this when the app behind them is unreachable.

A refusal comes back in about a millisecond. On a timeout, your machine resends the SYN a few times, waiting longer each time, before it gives up. So even the waiting is a clue.

Each tool in your toolbox answers one question:

- `ping`: are you there? It uses ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), a small protocol for network status messages that many firewalls block, so a failed ping proves little.
- `traceroute`: which routers does my traffic pass on the way?
- `dig` and `nslookup`: what does DNS say about this name?
- `ifconfig` on a Mac, `ip addr` on Linux: which addresses do I have?
- `lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` on a Mac, `ss -tlnp` on Linux: who listens on which port?
- `nc -zv host port`: can I open a TCP connection to that port?

`ss` and `ip` exist only on Linux. Use them in your practice box, where `apt install iproute2` adds them.

lessons.analogy: Connecting to a service is like mailing a letter to a business you only know by name. First you look up its street address in a phone book (DNS). The street address finds the building (the IP address), and the apartment number finds the right person inside (the port). Registered mail with receipts is TCP, and a postcard is UDP. Your home's front desk rewrites the return address on every outgoing letter to the building's address, and remembers who sent what (NAT). Real mail takes days, and this takes milliseconds. There is also no single phone book: copies of it sit in caches all over the world, and any of them may be a little out of date.

worked.title: Debug a service name that does not resolve

steps.say: A Redis container called cache runs on a Docker network called shopnet. Redis is the small database hello-devops can use to count visits. A Docker network is a private network that containers join (Day 20), and `-d` runs a container in the background. A second container, client, stands in for your app, and it starts on Docker's default network. Inside client, install three tools: dig (in dnsutils), ip and nc. The first two docker commands print long IDs, trimmed here.
steps.code:
$ docker network create shopnet
$ docker run -d --name cache --network shopnet redis:8-alpine
$ docker run -it --rm --name client --hostname client ubuntu:24.04 bash
root@client:/# apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq dnsutils iproute2 netcat-openbsd > /dev/null
debconf: delaying package configuration, since apt-utils is not installed

steps.say: Reproduce the symptom. Your colleague says the app cannot reach cache on port 6379. Try it with nc. Read the error carefully: getaddrinfo is the function programs call to look up a name. It failed before a single packet went to port 6379, so this is a DNS problem, not a firewall or a dead Redis.
steps.code:
root@client:/# nc -zv cache 6379
nc: getaddrinfo for host "cache" port 6379: Name or service not known

steps.say: Ask the system resolver the way apps do, with `getent hosts`. It reads /etc/hosts and then DNS. When the name is unknown, it prints nothing and exits with code 2. The hosts file only knows localhost and the container itself (IPv6 lines trimmed). So the DNS server this container uses has never heard of cache.
steps.code:
root@client:/# getent hosts cache; echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 2
root@client:/# cat /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1	localhost
172.17.0.3	client

steps.say: In a second Mac terminal, compare the two containers' networks. Docker answers container names through a built-in DNS server, but only on user-made networks, and only for containers on the same network. The client container sits on the default network, called bridge, so it cannot see the shopnet phone book.
steps.code:
$ docker inspect -f '{{range $k, $v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' cache
shopnet
$ docker inspect -f '{{range $k, $v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' client
bridge

steps.say: Fix it by connecting client to shopnet. Back inside client, the resolver has changed to 127.0.0.11, Docker's built-in DNS server, and the name now resolves.
steps.code:
$ docker network connect shopnet client

root@client:/# grep nameserver /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 127.0.0.11
root@client:/# getent hosts cache
172.20.0.2      cache

steps.say: Read the DNS answer with dig, then test the ports. The answer line has five columns: name, TTL in seconds, class (IN, for internet), type (A) and the address. Port 6379 succeeds. Port 6380 is refused at once: the host is there, but nothing listens on that port.
steps.code:
root@client:/# dig +noall +answer cache
cache.			600	IN	A	172.20.0.2
root@client:/# nc -zv cache 6379
Connection to cache (172.20.0.2) 6379 port [tcp/redis] succeeded!
root@client:/# nc -zv cache 6380
nc: connect to cache (172.20.0.2) port 6380 (tcp) failed: Connection refused

steps.say: Look at what changed underneath. client now has two addresses, one per network, each in a /16. Its route table sends each /16 straight out of the matching interface and everything else to the default gateway. That is the route table from this lesson, for real, though your addresses will differ. Exit and clean up with `docker rm -f cache` and `docker network rm shopnet`.
steps.code:
root@client:/# ip -4 addr | grep inet
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
    inet 172.17.0.3/16 brd 172.17.255.255 scope global eth0
    inet 172.20.0.3/16 brd 172.20.255.255 scope global eth1
root@client:/# ip route
default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0
172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.3
172.20.0.0/16 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link src 172.20.0.3

code.title: netcheck.py
code.src:
"""netcheck.py: can I reach HOST on PORT? If not, which step failed?

Usage: python3 netcheck.py HOST PORT
"""

import socket
import sys
import time


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("usage: python3 netcheck.py HOST PORT")
        return 2
    host, port = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])

    # Step 1: turn the name into an address, with the same resolver apps use
    # (/etc/hosts first, then DNS).
    try:
        ip = socket.gethostbyname(host)
    except socket.gaierror as err:
        print(f"DNS FAIL  {host} does not resolve ({err.strerror})")
        return 1
    print(f"DNS OK    {host} -> {ip}")

    # Step 2: open a TCP connection (the three-way handshake).
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((ip, port), timeout=3):
            ms = (time.monotonic() - start) * 1000
            print(f"TCP OK    {ip}:{port} accepted the connection in {ms:.0f} ms")
            return 0
    except ConnectionRefusedError:
        print(f"REFUSED   {ip}:{port} answered, but no program listens on that port")
    except socket.timeout:
        print(f"TIMEOUT   {ip}:{port} sent no answer in 3 s (firewall drop or wrong address)")
    except OSError as err:
        print(f"ERROR     {ip}:{port} {err.strerror}")
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

lessons.mistake: When one service cannot reach another, people restart things and change firewall rules at random. Read the error first. "Name or service not known" means DNS. "Refused" means nothing listens on that port. A timeout means something drops the packets, or the address is wrong. Each points to a different fix, and `nc -zv` or `netcheck.py` tells you which one you have in seconds.
lessons.real_world: A team is moving its ledger database to a new server behind the name `ledger-db.internal`. A day early, they lower that record's TTL from one hour to 60 seconds, so every client picks up the new address within a minute of the switch. After the move, they raise the TTL again to cut the number of DNS queries.

task.title: Take your own network apart
steps: Find your laptop's private address and your default gateway. Then find your public address. Write down which range the private one is in, and why the two differ.
Read the netmask from `ifconfig en0` and turn it into a /N. Use Python's `ipaddress` to count the addresses in your home network, and to check whether 10.0.3.7 is inside 10.0.2.0/23.
Use dig to find the A, AAAA, MX, NS and TXT records of a domain you use. Run `dig @1.1.1.1 github.com` twice, a few seconds apart, and compare the TTLs.
Run `dig +trace example.com` and name the three kinds of server it talks to, in order.
Add the line `127.0.0.1 myapp.test` to /etc/hosts. Compare `ping -c 1 myapp.test` with `dig +short myapp.test`, explain the difference, then remove the line.

Start two throwaway servers: `python3 -m http.server 9101 --bind 127.0.0.1` and `python3 -m http.server 9102 --bind 0.0.0.0`. Compare them in `lsof`, then try to reach both through your private address.
Save `netcheck.py` from this lesson in `~/code/netlab`. Make it print each of its four results: TCP OK, REFUSED, DNS FAIL and TIMEOUT.
For each of the four results, write one line: which step failed, and what you would check next.
hints: Editing /etc/hosts needs sudo: `sudo sh -c 'echo "127.0.0.1 myapp.test" >> /etc/hosts'`, and later `sudo sed -i '' '/myapp.test/d' /etc/hosts` removes it.
For REFUSED, try a port where nothing runs. For TIMEOUT, try an address that does not exist on your network, such as 10.255.255.1 port 443; some routers answer 'no route' instead.
A 0xffffff00 netmask has 24 bits set, so it is a /24.
task.done_when: You are done when netcheck.py has printed TCP OK, REFUSED, DNS FAIL and TIMEOUT (or a 'no route' error) for four targets, and you can say which step failed each time.

explain_back.prompt: Explain, step by step, what happens when an app connects to `cache:6379`. Mention the resolver, the IP address, the port and the TCP handshake.
explain_back.answer: First the app asks the operating system's resolver for the address of cache. It checks /etc/hosts and its cache, then asks a DNS server, such as Docker's built-in one at 127.0.0.11. With the IP address in hand, the app sends a SYN to that address on port 6379. The server answers SYN-ACK, the app sends ACK, and the TCP connection is open. If the name is unknown, it fails before any packet is sent. If nothing listens on 6379, the connection is refused, and if a firewall drops the packets, it times out.

recap: An IP address finds the machine and a port finds the program; private ranges reach the internet through NAT.
/N fixes N bits: /24 is 256 addresses, /16 is 65,536, and a bigger N means a smaller network.
Bind to 0.0.0.0 inside containers; publish to 127.0.0.1 when only your laptop should connect.
DNS goes from the stub resolver to a recursive resolver, then root, TLD and authoritative servers, caching each answer for its TTL.
Unresolved means DNS, refused means no listener, and a timeout means a drop or a wrong address.

check.q: A teammate's app listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 inside a container started with `-p 8080:8080`, and nobody can reach it. What do you suggest?
options: Publish port 80 instead of port 8080
Add the container's name to /etc/hosts
Switch the app from TCP to UDP
Bind the app to 0.0.0.0 in the container
check.why: Docker forwards published ports to the container's network address, and an app bound to loopback never sees that traffic.

check.q: `nc -zv db.internal 22` succeeds at once, but `nc -zv db.internal 5432` waits 30 seconds and then times out. What is the most likely cause?
options: A firewall drops traffic to port 5432
DNS has no record for db.internal
PostgreSQL is stopped on the server
The server's disk is completely full
check.why: The name resolves and the host answers on port 22, and a stopped database would be refused fast, so silence points to dropped packets.

check.q: Your network is 10.0.0.0/16 and you need four subnets of equal size, as large as possible. Which prefix do they get?
check.why: Four equal parts need two more fixed bits, so 16 + 2 = /18, with 16,384 addresses each.

interview.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP, and when would you pick each?
interview.a: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake, then delivers bytes in order and resends anything lost. That suits HTTP, SSH and databases, where every byte matters. UDP just sends independent datagrams with no setup and no delivery promise, so it is lighter and has less delay. It suits small request-response protocols like DNS, and live audio or video, where a late packet is useless anyway. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP and builds its own reliability on top.

interview.q: A service logs 'connection refused' when it calls another service. How do you debug it?
interview.a: Refused means DNS worked and the target host answered, but nothing accepted the connection on that port. So I check the target: is the process running, which port does it listen on, and is it bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0? On the target I would run `ss -tlnp` to see the listeners. From the caller I would run `nc -zv` against the exact host and port from the config, to rule out a typo in the port.

interview.q: Walk me through DNS resolution for a name nobody on your network has looked up recently.
interview.a: The app asks the operating system's stub resolver, which checks /etc/hosts and its cache, then forwards the query to a recursive resolver. With an empty cache, the recursive resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the TLD servers, such as those for .com. The TLD server refers it to the domain's authoritative name servers, which return the record. The recursive resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it, and the stub resolver may cache it too.

deeper.body:
`dig +trace example.com` lets you play recursive resolver yourself. Instead of asking your usual resolver for a finished answer, dig starts at the top and follows each referral. You see three blocks of output:

1. A list of root servers, named `a.root-servers.net` to `m.root-servers.net`. dig asks one of them about example.com.
2. The root does not know the answer, but it knows who runs .com. It returns NS records for the .com servers. dig asks one of those.
3. The .com server returns the NS records for example.com's own name servers. dig asks one of them and finally gets the A record.

Each block ends with a line saying which server answered and how long it took. Every step is a referral to a server lower in the tree. Your recursive resolver does exactly this when its cache is empty, and caches each referral so the next lookup skips most of the trip.

Real resolvers add two complications:

- Negative answers are cached too. If you look up a name before its record exists, resolvers can remember "no such name" for a while, so a record you just created can still look missing.
- Flushing your own cache only fixes your machine. On a Mac, `sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder` clears the local cache, but your router's and your provider's caches keep the old answer until the TTL ends.

If you want to watch DNS from the other side, try [Mess With DNS](https://messwithdns.net/about.html) by Julia Evans. It gives you a real subdomain to create records on and shows the queries arriving live, so you can create an A record, `dig` it, and see the question land. Records are deleted after a week.

Last, a trap on the Mac: the name `localhost` can resolve to the IPv6 loopback `::1` as well as `127.0.0.1`. curl tries both, but some tools only try the first. If a server bound to `127.0.0.1` looks down from one tool and up from another, connect to `127.0.0.1` explicitly and compare.

sections.h: HTTP is text with a strict shape
sections.body:
HTTP is the language browsers, curl and apps use to talk to web servers. It runs on top of a TCP connection, which you met on Day 10. The client sends a request, and the server sends back exactly one response.

In HTTP/1.1 both are plain text. A request has four parts, in this order:

1. A request line: the method, the path and the version, such as `GET /healthz HTTP/1.1`.
2. Headers: one `Name: value` per line, such as `Host: localhost:8000`.
3. A blank line, which says the headers are over.
4. An optional body: the data you send, such as JSON for a POST.

A response has the same shape, with a status line first: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`. You can see both halves with `curl -v`. Lines starting with `>` are what curl sent, and lines starting with `<` came back.

Because it is text, you could type a request by hand. `printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc example.com 80` does exactly that. The `\r\n` pairs are the line endings HTTP requires.

HTTP is stateless: the server treats each request on its own and does not remember the last one. Logins still work because of cookies. The server sends a `Set-Cookie` header with a token, and the browser sends it back in a `Cookie` header on every later request.

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep the same methods, headers and status codes. An HTTP/1.1 connection carries one request at a time, so browsers open several. HTTP/2 runs many requests at once over one TCP connection, packed into binary frames. But TCP delivers bytes in order (Day 10), so one lost packet stalls them all. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, on UDP, where a lost packet stalls only its own request. For debugging you can think in HTTP/1.1 terms, because curl shows you the same fields.

sections.h: Methods, and why idempotency matters
sections.body:
The method says what you want to do:

- GET: read something. It should change nothing.
- POST: create something or submit data, such as a payment.
- PUT: replace something with the body you send.
- PATCH: change part of something.
- DELETE: remove something.
- HEAD: like GET, but return only the headers.
- OPTIONS: ask what is allowed. Browsers send it before some cross-site requests.

A safe method changes nothing on the server: GET and HEAD. An **idempotent** method has the same effect whether you send it once or five times: GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE. Deleting order 42 twice leaves it just as deleted.

POST is neither. Send "charge this card 20 euros" twice, and you may charge twice.

Operators care about this because networks fail halfway. A client sends a request, the connection drops, and nobody knows whether the server got it. Retrying an idempotent request is safe. Retrying a POST is not, unless the API gives you a way to make it safe. Payment APIs often accept an idempotency key: a unique ID per payment, so the server can ignore a repeat. Proxies know this too. nginx, for example, will not retry a POST on another server by default once it has sent it to one.

sections.h: Status codes: what each one tells an operator
sections.body:
Every response starts with a three-digit status code. The first digit gives the family, so even a client that does not know a code can act on it:

- 1xx: information, rarely seen.
- 2xx: success.
- 3xx: go somewhere else.
- 4xx: the client did something wrong.
- 5xx: the server side failed.

The ones you will read in logs and dashboards, and what each suggests:

- 200 OK and 201 Created: it worked. 201 means a POST made something new.
- 301 and 302: redirects. The `Location` header says where to go, and 301 is permanent.
- 304 Not Modified: your cached copy is still good, so no body is sent.
- 400 Bad Request: the request itself is broken, such as invalid JSON.
- 401 Unauthorized: who are you? Despite the name, it means credentials are missing or wrong.
- 403 Forbidden: I know who you are, and you may not do this.
- 404 Not Found: no such path. Look for a typo or a missing route.
- 429 Too Many Requests: slow down, because a rate limit kicked in.
- 500 Internal Server Error: the app crashed or threw an exception.
- 502 Bad Gateway: a proxy could not get a good answer from the app behind it.
- 503 Service Unavailable: the server is up but cannot serve right now, like hello-devops's `/readyz` while Redis is down.
- 504 Gateway Timeout: a proxy waited for the app and gave up.

The last three, 502, 503 and 504, usually come from a proxy or load balancer, not from your code. "Gateway" in their names means that server in the middle. A 502 means the app was unreachable or answered with garbage. You will cause one on purpose in today's hands-on.

sections.h: Headers that matter, and curl as your microscope
sections.body:
Headers carry the details. A few matter every day:

- `Host`: which site you want. One server address can host many sites, and this header picks one.
- `Content-Type`: what the body is, such as `application/json`.
- `Authorization`: credentials, such as a bearer token (whoever holds it gets in). Never write it to a log.
- `Cache-Control`: who may cache the response, and for how long.
- `X-Forwarded-For`: the original client's address, added by proxies along the way.

A handful of curl flags cover nearly everything:

- `-v` shows the whole conversation, including the DNS, TCP and TLS steps.
- `-i` prints the response headers with the body, and `-I` sends a HEAD request for headers only.
- `-L` follows redirects.
- `-X`, `-H` and `-d` set the method, add a header and send a body.
- `-o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}'` prints only the status code, which is handy in scripts.
- `-w` with timing variables shows how long DNS, connect, TLS and the first byte took.
- `--resolve name:port:address` skips DNS and sends that name to an address you choose.

With `--resolve` you can test a new server under its real name before you change DNS, because the `Host` header and TLS still use the name from the URL.

sections.h: TLS: what HTTPS adds
sections.body:
Plain HTTP is readable text, and every router between you and the server (Day 10) passes it along. Whoever runs one of them, or shares an open café Wi-Fi with you, could read a password or change the page. HTTPS is HTTP inside a TLS connection. TLS (Transport Layer Security) gives you three things:

- Confidentiality: nobody on the path can read the traffic.
- Integrity: nobody can change it without the change being detected.
- Authentication: the server proves it holds the private key for a certificate that names this host.

Before any HTTP flows, the client and the server run a handshake. In TLS 1.3, the current version, it takes one round trip:

1. The client sends ClientHello. It lists the ciphers (encryption methods) it supports and its half of a key exchange. It also names the host it wants, in a field called SNI (Server Name Indication), which is TLS's version of the Host header. It lists the HTTP versions it speaks too, called ALPN.
2. The server answers with ServerHello and its half of the key exchange. Then, already encrypted, it sends its certificate and a signature that proves it holds the matching private key.
3. The client checks the certificate: the right name, still valid, and signed by someone it trusts.
4. Both sides compute the same session keys from the two halves. Everything after this, including the HTTP request, is encrypted.

How can two machines agree on a key while others listen? Each side keeps a random secret and sends only a public value made from it. Each combines its own secret with the other's public value, and both arrive at the same key. The public values alone are not enough to work it out.

The signature in step 2 is the same proof your SSH key gave on Day 7. Only the private key can make it, and anyone with the public key can check it.

TLS does not hide everything. The server's IP address is visible to everyone on the path, and usually so is the host name, because SNI is sent before encryption starts.

sections.h: Certificates, CAs and Let's Encrypt
sections.body:
The signature only proves the server holds some private key. How does your browser know that key belongs to github.com, and not to an attacker? On Day 7, ssh asked you to accept a new server's fingerprint. A browser cannot ask you about every site, so it trusts a few certificate authorities (CAs) to vouch for servers.

A certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to these names, from this date to that date". The names live in a field called Subject Alternative Name (SAN), such as `DNS:localhost`. A CA signs it after checking that the requester controls those names.

Your operating system and browser ship a trust store: a list of root CAs they trust. Roots rarely sign server certificates directly. They sign intermediate CAs, and an intermediate signs the server's certificate. That lets the root keys stay offline, locked away. The server sends its certificate plus the intermediates, and the client follows that chain up to a root it already trusts. If any link is missing, expired or made out to another name, the connection fails.

Let's Encrypt is a free CA run by a non-profit. It issues certificates automatically through a protocol called ACME. To prove you control a domain, you pass a challenge:

- HTTP-01: serve a token at a known URL on port 80. It cannot give you a wildcard certificate.
- DNS-01: publish a TXT record. It is the only way to get a wildcard such as `*.example.com`.

Both prove control of the name. For HTTP-01, Let's Encrypt fetches the token from whatever server the name points to. For DNS-01, it reads the record from the domain's own DNS.

Certificates expire, which limits how long a stolen key stays useful, and on purpose they expire sooner each year. Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days today, and 45 days from 2028 (Go deeper has the dates). Nobody should renew those by hand, so renewal must be automated and watched.

The padlock proves less than people think. Let's Encrypt gives a certificate to anyone who controls a domain, including `paypa1-login.example`. TLS says "you are talking privately to whoever controls this name", and nothing about whether they are honest.

For `localhost`, no public CA will issue a certificate, because nobody uniquely owns that name. You make your own, as in the worked example.

sections.h: Proxies, load balancers and the rest of the path
sections.body:
In production, a request rarely goes straight to your app. Picture hello-devops on one server with a public address: one crash takes the site down, and each new copy needs its own address and certificate. So requests pass through servers in the middle.

A **reverse proxy** sits in front of your apps and receives every request on their behalf, then forwards each one to an app behind it. Common ones are nginx, Envoy, Caddy and Traefik. A forward proxy is the opposite: it acts for clients, such as a company proxy that all outgoing traffic must pass through.

Reverse proxies take on jobs each app should not repeat:

- TLS termination: the proxy holds the certificate and talks plain HTTP to the apps behind it.
- Routing by host or path: `/api` goes to one service and `/` to another.
- Load balancing: spreading requests across several copies of an app.
- Health checks: probing each copy, for example with `GET /healthz`, and skipping the ones that fail.
- Rate limiting: answering 429 when one client sends too much.

nginx calls the app servers behind it upstreams, and today's `lb.conf` lists them in an `upstream` block.

A load balancer works at one of two levels, numbered after the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model of network layers. Layer 4 is TCP and UDP with their ports, and layer 7 is the application's protocol, such as HTTP. A layer 4 balancer sees only addresses and ports and forwards whole TCP connections, so it is fast and works for any protocol. A layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request, so it can route on paths, headers and cookies. An L7 balancer is really a reverse proxy with several backends. Sticky sessions are an L7 feature: one user keeps landing on the same copy, usually through a cookie. I would rather keep apps free of in-memory state, so any copy can serve any request. Today's task shows why: with `REDIS_HOST` empty, each copy of hello-devops counts visits in its own memory, so the two copies disagree.

Two more pieces sit further out. A CDN (content delivery network) is a worldwide set of caching proxies that serves copies of your files from near the user, and `Cache-Control` says what it may keep. A firewall allows or denies traffic by address, port and protocol before it reaches the proxy.

lessons.analogy: A reverse proxy is the receptionist of an office building. Every visitor talks to the receptionist first. The receptionist checks their papers at the door (TLS termination), looks at what they want (the path and headers) and walks them to a free clerk (load balancing). If no clerk is at a desk, the receptionist says so: that is the 502. TLS is the sealed envelope plus the check of the building's papers on the way in. A real receptionist remembers yesterday's visitors. The server does not: it forgets each request once it has answered, unless a cookie reminds it.

steps.say: Make a folder and a certificate for localhost. Your Mac's openssl is a different build (LibreSSL) with different flags, so run real OpenSSL from the python:3.14-slim image instead. The flag `-x509` makes a self-signed certificate, `-nodes` leaves the key unencrypted, and `-addext` adds the names. While it makes the key, openssl prints a line of dots and plus signs; that is normal.
steps.code:
$ mkdir -p ~/code/netlab/tls && cd ~/code/netlab/tls
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/certs -w /certs python:3.14-slim \
    openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout localhost.key -out localhost.crt \
    -days 7 -subj /CN=localhost -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1"
$ ls
localhost.crt  localhost.key

Then start nginx with the config and the certificate mounted read-only. Only nginx publishes a port, and only on 127.0.0.1, so the app is reachable through nginx alone.

$ docker network create weblab
$ docker run -d --rm --name whoami --network weblab traefik/whoami
$ docker run -d --rm --name tls --network weblab -p 127.0.0.1:8443:443 \
    -v "$PWD/tls.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro" -v "$PWD:/etc/nginx/certs:ro" nginx:alpine

X-Forwarded-Proto says the client used https, though the app only saw plain HTTP.

Then the server's hello, its certificate and its proof of the key. Last, the agreed TLS version and cipher, and the certificate check passing on name and dates. Your Mac's curl words these lines a little differently.

lessons.mistake: Adding `-k` to make a certificate error go away (or the same switch in your HTTP library) turns off the identity check. With it, curl talks to an attacker just as happily, and the setting tends to reach production. Fix the trust instead: give the tool the right CA file with `--cacert`, fix the server's chain, or use the right host name.
lessons.real_world: Every public request to a payments API first reaches a layer 7 load balancer, which holds the TLS certificates and renews them on its own. The balancer routes `/api/payments` to the payments service and spreads requests over copies in two zones. Health checks tell it which copies to skip. The API also requires an idempotency key on every POST, so a retry after a dropped connection never charges a card twice.

task.title: Load-balance two copies of hello-devops
steps: Make `~/code/netlab/lb`, save `lb.conf` from this lesson there, and create a Docker network called `netlab`.

Start app1 from your hello-devops folder: `docker run -d --name app1 --network netlab -e GREETING="Hello from app1" -v ~/code/hello-devops:/app:ro -w /app python:3.14-slim sh -c "pip install -q -r requirements.txt && python app.py"`. Start app2 the same way, with its own name and greeting.
Wait until `docker logs app1` and `docker logs app2` both show "Running on all addresses (0.0.0.0)". Explain to yourself why that line matters.
Start nginx as a container called `proxy` on the same network, with `lb.conf` mounted and port 8080 published on 127.0.0.1 only.
Send ten requests to `localhost:8080` and count how many each copy answered. Is it a perfect 5 and 5?
Send a POST and a request for a path that does not exist. Write down both status codes and which side (client or server) each one blames.
Stop app2. Time the next few requests with `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' localhost:8080/`. Explain the slow one, using the comments in `lb.conf`.
Stop app1 too. Get a 502, then find the reason in `docker logs proxy`.
Clean up the three containers and the network.
hints: Counting: `for i in $(seq 10); do curl -s localhost:8080/ | jq -r .message; done | sort | uniq -c` uses the Part 1 tools you already know.
If nginx exits at once with "host not found in upstream", it started before app1 or app2 existed. Start the apps first, then nginx.
`docker stop app2` takes about 10 seconds because Python, running as PID 1 in the container, ignores SIGTERM, so Docker waits and then sends SIGKILL (Day 6).
task.done_when: You are done when you have seen answers from both app1 and app2 through localhost:8080, then a 502 Bad Gateway after stopping both, and you can explain each result.

explain_back.prompt: Explain what nginx did for one request in today's labs, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention TLS termination, the upstream and what a 502 means.
explain_back.answer: nginx received the client's HTTPS connection on port 443, ran the TLS handshake with its certificate and decrypted the request, which is TLS termination. It then picked one of the upstream servers, app1 or app2, and forwarded the request over plain HTTP on port 8000. On the way it added X-Forwarded-For, so the app knows the real client. When an upstream did not answer within the connect timeout, nginx tried the other one. When no upstream could answer, nginx itself replied 502 Bad Gateway, which means the proxy was fine but the app behind it was not.

recap: An HTTP message is a start line, headers, a blank line and an optional body, and `curl -v` shows all of it.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent and safe to retry; POST is not, unless the API takes an idempotency key.
4xx blames the client and 5xx the server; 502, 503 and 504 usually come from proxies.
TLS encrypts and proves control of a name; the client follows the certificate chain to a trusted root.
Certificates are getting shorter-lived, so renewal must be automated and monitored.
A reverse proxy ends TLS, routes and load-balances; L4 sees ports, L7 sees HTTP.

check.q: During a slow database migration, users get 504 Gateway Timeout from the load balancer. What does that tell you first?
options: The app answers too slowly, not that it is down
The users' browsers sent broken requests
The TLS certificate on the balancer expired
DNS points the domain at the wrong address
check.why: 504 means the proxy reached the app but gave up waiting for an answer, which fits a slow database.

check.q: A POST /payments request timed out, the client retried it, and the customer was charged twice. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Change the method from POST to GET
Turn off retries in every client
Raise the proxy's timeout to 5 minutes
Send an idempotency key the server checks
check.why: POST is not idempotent, so the server needs a unique key per payment to recognise and ignore the repeat.

check.q: A logged-in user tries to delete another team's project. The API answers 401. Which code fits better?
options: 400 Bad Request
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
500 Server Error
check.why: 401 means 'who are you?'. This user is known but not allowed, which is what 403 says.

interview.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?
interview.a: The browser resolves the host name through DNS, using a cached answer if it has one. It opens a TCP connection to that address on port 443 and runs a TLS handshake. In the handshake, the server proves its identity with a certificate, which the browser checks against its trust store. It then sends an HTTP GET, usually to a load balancer or reverse proxy that ends TLS and forwards the request to one healthy app server. The response comes back with a status code, headers and a body, and the browser renders the page and fetches whatever else it references.

interview.q: What is the difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?
interview.a: A layer 4 balancer works with IP addresses and ports and forwards whole TCP or UDP connections without reading their contents. It is fast and protocol-agnostic. A layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can route by host, path, headers or cookies, end TLS, add headers like X-Forwarded-For and run HTTP health checks. I would use L7 for web traffic and L4 for things like databases or custom TCP protocols.

interview.q: What is TLS termination, and where would you do it?
interview.a: TLS termination means a proxy or load balancer decrypts HTTPS and passes the request on, often as plain HTTP. It keeps certificates and renewal in one place and lets the proxy route on HTTP details. The trade-off is that traffic behind the proxy is unencrypted unless you re-encrypt it. In a shared or regulated network, I would use TLS to the backends too. Most teams terminate at the edge load balancer or the Kubernetes gateway.

deeper.body:
Certificate lifetimes are shrinking on a schedule, and it changes how operators work. Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days today. Its default profile moves to 64 days on February 10, 2027, and to 45 days on February 16, 2028. An opt-in profile already issues 45-day certificates, and another issues certificates that last about six days. Industry rules will cap every public certificate at 47 days from March 15, 2029. The plans and the reasons are in Let's Encrypt's [certificate lifetimes page](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/cert-lifetimes/).

What this means in practice:

- Never renew by hand. Use an ACME client that renews on its own, or a platform feature that does, such as cert-manager in Kubernetes.
- Renew early. Let's Encrypt suggests renewing at about two thirds of a certificate's lifetime, or following its renewal-information service, called ARI.
- Hunt for hard-coded intervals. A cron job that renews every 60 or 80 days will break when certificates last 45. Let's Encrypt suggests grepping for those numbers.
- Monitor expiry anyway. `openssl x509 -noout -checkend 1209600` exits non-zero when a certificate expires within 14 days, which makes a simple alert.

Two more changes make old tutorials wrong. First, Let's Encrypt switched off its OCSP service on August 6, 2025, and now publishes revocation only through certificate revocation lists (CRLs). Guides that run `openssl ocsp` against Let's Encrypt are out of date. Second, Let's Encrypt announced a new chain of root and intermediate CAs in late 2025. So do not hard-code intermediate names such as R3 or R10 in scripts or firewall rules, because the names change.

If you want the mechanics of the handshake in more depth, the TLS chapter of [High Performance Browser Networking](https://hpbn.co/transport-layer-security-tls/) is free and still clear. It was written before TLS 1.3, so remember that 1.3 cut the handshake to one round trip.

lessons.goal: By the end you can describe what a cloud provider rents you, design a small two-zone network with subnets, routes and firewalls, write a least-privilege policy, and avoid a surprise bill.

options: AWS stops the servers when you reach $5
AWS deletes the servers and keeps your data
Your bill is capped at $5 for that month
You get an email, and the servers keep running
guess.why: A budget alert only notifies you. The servers keep running and billing until you delete them.

terms.plain: A geographic area where a cloud provider runs data centers, such as Frankfurt.
One or more separate data centers inside a region, with their own power and network.
Virtual private cloud: your own private network inside a cloud provider, with a CIDR block you choose.
A smaller block of addresses inside a VPC; in AWS each subnet lives in one availability zone.
A stateful, allow-only firewall attached to a cloud machine's network interface.
A set of permissions that a person or a machine takes on for a while, with credentials that expire.
Giving each person or job only the permissions it needs, and nothing more.
The split of security work: the provider secures the cloud itself, and you secure what you put in it.

sections.h: What the cloud is
sections.body:
Before the cloud, a team that needed a new server bought one, waited for it to be delivered and installed, and paid for it whether it was busy or idle. The cloud is renting computers, storage and ready-made services from a provider, by the second or the hour. You never see the hardware. You ask for a machine on a website or through an API, and a minute later it exists. When you delete it, the bill for it stops.

Every click in a cloud console, the provider's website, is really an API call, so anything you can click, a program can do. Terraform (Part 8) creates cloud resources from code by calling the same APIs, and a pipeline can run Terraform.

Cloud services differ in how much the provider runs for you:

- IaaS (infrastructure as a service): you rent virtual machines, disks and networks, and you install and patch the operating system. Example: AWS EC2.
- PaaS (platform as a service): you hand over code or a container, and the provider runs it. Examples: Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps.
- SaaS (software as a service): finished software that you just use, such as GitHub or Gmail.
- Serverless functions: you upload one function, it runs on each event, and you pay per request and for the time it runs. It scales to zero: when no events arrive, nothing runs and you pay nothing for compute. Example: AWS Lambda.

Managed services sit in between. A managed database such as AWS RDS gives you PostgreSQL without you running the server: the provider patches it, backs it up and fails it over. You still own the schema, the queries and who may connect.

refs.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner course, CLF-C02 (freeCodeCamp)

sections.h: Regions and availability zones
sections.body:
Providers group their data centers by place. A **region** is a geographic area, such as AWS's `eu-central-1` in Frankfurt or Google's `us-central1` in Iowa. Inside a region sit several availability zones (AZs). AWS describes an AZ as one or more separate data centers with their own power, networking and connectivity, linked to the other AZs by fast private fiber.

The split exists because things fail at every size:

- One server dies: run two copies.
- One data center loses power or floods: run copies in two or more AZs.
- A whole region has a bad day: rare, and only the most critical systems plan for it.

For most apps, two or three AZs in one region is the right amount. The AZs are close enough for fast traffic between them and far enough apart not to fail together.

To pick a region, answer three questions:

1. Where are your users? Closer means lower latency, the delay before an answer arrives.
2. Where must the data live? Laws and contracts can require a country or region.
3. What does it cost? Prices differ between regions.

A cloud console shows one region at a time, and nearly every beginner gets caught by this. A server you created in another region keeps running and billing, out of sight. Pick one region for all your learning and stay there.

refs.title: AWS Regions and Availability Zones (AWS docs)

sections.h: The core service map across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
sections.body:
The three big providers sell the same kinds of building blocks under different names. Running hello-devops in the cloud would take one service from most of these lines, from a machine to run it to DNS for its name. Learn the category first, and the names follow:

- Virtual machines: EC2 (AWS), Virtual Machines (Azure), Compute Engine (Google Cloud).
- Managed Kubernetes: EKS, AKS, GKE.
- Containers without a cluster: Fargate, Container Apps, Cloud Run.
- Functions: Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions.
- Object storage, for files you read and write whole over HTTPS: S3, Blob Storage, Cloud Storage.
- Managed SQL databases: RDS, Azure SQL Database and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL.
- Private networks: VPC, Virtual Network (VNet), VPC.
- DNS: Route 53, Azure DNS, Cloud DNS.
- Load balancers: Elastic Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway, Cloud Load Balancing.
- Identity and access: IAM, Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC, Cloud IAM.
- Monitoring and logs: CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.

Similar names do not mean identical behaviour, and Google's own comparison page warns about this. One example: in Google Cloud a VPC network is global and its subnets are regional, while an AWS VPC lives in a single region.

Names also change. Google's Cloud Functions became Cloud Run functions, for example. Check the current docs before you trust any table, including this one.

sections.h: Networking in the cloud: VPCs, subnets and routes
sections.body:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your own private network inside the provider. Everything from Day 10 comes back here, except that now you set it up yourself.

You give the VPC a private CIDR block, such as `10.0.0.0/16`. Then you split it into subnets: smaller blocks such as `10.0.1.0/24`. In AWS each subnet lives in exactly one AZ, so an app in two AZs needs subnets in both. AWS also keeps 5 addresses in every subnet (the first four and the last), for jobs such as the VPC's router and DNS. So a /24 gives you 251 usable addresses, not 256.

What makes a subnet public or private is its route table, not its name:

- Every route table has a local route, such as `10.0.0.0/16` to `local`, so all subnets in the VPC can reach each other.
- A public subnet adds `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway. `0.0.0.0/0` means every address, so this is the default route. Machines here can have public addresses and be reached from the internet.
- A private subnet adds `0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT gateway instead. Its machines can reach out, for example to download packages, but nobody outside can start a connection to them.

Day 10's rule picks between routes: `10.0.0.0/16` is more specific than `0.0.0.0/0`, so traffic between subnets stays inside the VPC.

This is your home router from Day 10 again, split in two. The internet gateway is the VPC's front door. A machine inside knows only its private address, so the gateway swaps in that machine's own public address, one for one. The NAT gateway does the home router's trick: many private machines share its single public address, and only replies get back in.

The usual layout puts load balancers in public subnets, and apps and databases in private ones. A machine in a private subnet has no public address and no route in from the internet, so even a wrong firewall rule cannot expose it directly.

sections.h: Cloud firewalls: security groups and network ACLs
sections.body:
AWS gives you two firewalls, and they behave differently. Mixing them up leads to a classic puzzle: the request arrives, but the reply never gets back.

A security group is a firewall attached to each machine (more exactly, to its network interface). Its rules only allow, and anything not allowed is blocked. It is stateful: it tracks connections, so the reply to an allowed request gets out without a rule of its own. A rule can also name another security group as its source. "Allow port 8000 from the load balancer's group" keeps working when the load balancer's addresses change.

A network ACL (NACL) guards a whole subnet. It is stateless: it judges every packet on its own, with no memory of connections. Its numbered rules can allow or deny, and the first match wins.

Stateless has a cost. Say a NACL allows inbound port 443. The server's reply goes back to the client's ephemeral port, somewhere between 1024 and 65535. If the NACL has no outbound rule for those ports, the reply is dropped. The request arrived, the app answered, and the client still times out. A security group would have let the reply out by itself.

AWS describes NACLs as a coarse, extra guard for whole subnets, and for most work security groups do the job. Azure's network security groups are stateful too. Whatever the cloud, start with nothing open and add only what each layer needs. Never open a database port to `0.0.0.0/0`.

sections.h: IAM: who may do what
sections.body:
Every API call can create, change or delete something, so the provider must know who is calling and what they may do. IAM (identity and access management) answers that for every call: may this caller do this action on this resource? The callers are called principals:

- Users: one person, with a console password or access keys (a long-lived ID and secret for programs).
- Groups: a set of users that share permissions.
- Roles: a set of permissions that a person or a machine takes on for a while. A CI job, a VM or a person assumes the role and gets temporary credentials that expire.

Permissions live in policies. In AWS a policy is a JSON document made of statements. Each statement has an Effect (allow or deny), an Action (such as `s3:GetObject`), a Resource (which bucket or object) and an optional Condition. Anything not allowed is denied.

The first rule that keeps you out of trouble is **least privilege**: grant only the actions and resources a job needs, then tighten from there. A deploy job that uploads to one bucket should not be able to delete databases. The second is to prefer roles over long-lived access keys. A key saved in a file or a CI secret works until someone deletes it, and a leaked key works for an attacker too. Role credentials expire on their own. Day 27 shows GitHub Actions getting cloud access this way, through a standard called OpenID Connect (OIDC), with no stored keys at all.

Security is shared between you and the provider. The provider secures the cloud itself: buildings, hardware and the virtualization layer. You secure what you put in it: your data, your IAM policies, your firewall rules and, on a VM, the operating system and its patches. The line moves with the service type. With serverless, the provider does nearly all of it; with a VM, patching the OS is your job.

sections.h: Pricing, free tiers and the cleanup habit
sections.body:
Cloud bills come from a few meters:

- Compute time, per second or hour, while a machine runs.
- Storage, per gigabyte per month, even for disks nobody uses.
- Requests, for services like object storage and functions.
- Data sent out to the internet (egress), per gigabyte.

You can buy compute three ways. On-demand is the default: no commitment and the highest price. Reserved capacity and savings plans give a discount for promising one or three years of use. Spot instances use spare capacity at a large discount, but the provider can take them back at short notice, so they suit work that can restart.

Some resources bill by the hour just for existing: NAT gateways, load balancers, public IPv4 addresses (scarce, as Day 10 showed), and disks or snapshots nobody uses. A stopped VM still pays for its disk.

Free tiers changed in 2025, and the rules in October 2026 look like this:

- AWS: new accounts pick a Free plan or a Paid plan. The Free plan gives $100 in credits plus up to $100 more for trying services, for 6 months or until the credits run out. Then the account closes instead of charging you. AWS's own FAQ disagrees with itself on when credits expire, so check the Credits page in your console.
- Azure: $200 of credit for 30 days, behind a spending limit that is on by default. Some services are free in limited amounts for 12 months, but after the 30 days you must upgrade to keep using them. Microsoft's pages disagree on how many services are always free (55 or 65).
- Google Cloud: $300 of credit for 90 days, and no charge until you activate a paid account. Separately, Always Free includes one small e2-micro VM, but only in three US regions.

These rules change, so read the provider's current page before you sign up. Then build the habit:

1. Set a budget alert on day one. It sends email; it does not stop anything.
2. Use one region, and tag everything with an owner and a purpose.
3. Delete what you made the same day. On Day 35 that is `terraform destroy`.
4. Never put access keys in code or in git.

Today needs no cloud account. Days 13 and 14 open one and use it by hand, and Day 35 builds on it with Terraform. All three are optional.

lessons.analogy: A VPC is your own fenced campus inside a huge rented business park. The park owner keeps the roads, the fences and the power running; you decide which buildings to put up, who gets a key card and which doors stay locked. A real campus charges it whether you use the place or not. The cloud bills by the hour for each thing that exists, so you can tear the whole campus down tonight and pay nothing tomorrow.

worked.title: Design PayFlow's checkout network on paper

steps.say: PayFlow, the made-up payments company, wants its checkout API in two AZs: a load balancer that the internet can reach, and the app and database that it cannot. Start with the VPC block. 10.0.0.0/16 gives 65,536 addresses, far more than needed, so there is room to add subnets for years. Python shows how it slices into /24s.
steps.code:
$ python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; print(list(i.ip_network('10.0.0.0/16').subnets(new_prefix=24))[:3])"
[IPv4Network('10.0.0.0/24'), IPv4Network('10.0.1.0/24'), IPv4Network('10.0.2.0/24')]

steps.say: Choose a numbering you can read at a glance. Public subnets get 10.0.1 and 10.0.2, private ones 10.0.11 and 10.0.12, and the letter is the AZ. Put that plan into `subnet_plan.py` and run it. Each /24 has 251 usable addresses in AWS, and nothing overlaps.
steps.code:
$ python3 subnet_plan.py
VPC 10.0.0.0/16: 65536 addresses
public-a   10.0.1.0/24     AZ a  public     251 usable  inside VPC
public-b   10.0.2.0/24     AZ b  public     251 usable  inside VPC
private-a  10.0.11.0/24    AZ a  private    251 usable  inside VPC
private-b  10.0.12.0/24    AZ b  private    251 usable  inside VPC
plan OK

steps.say: Break it on purpose, so you trust the check. Type private-b as 10.0.2.0/24, a copy-paste slip that really happens. Two subnets may never share addresses, and the script says so and exits with 1, which a CI job would treat as a failure.
steps.code:
$ python3 subnet_plan.py
VPC 10.0.0.0/16: 65536 addresses
public-a   10.0.1.0/24     AZ a  public     251 usable  inside VPC
public-b   10.0.2.0/24     AZ b  public     251 usable  inside VPC
private-a  10.0.11.0/24    AZ a  private    251 usable  inside VPC
private-b  10.0.2.0/24     AZ b  private    251 usable  inside VPC
OVERLAP   public-b 10.0.2.0/24 and private-b 10.0.2.0/24
plan has problems

steps.say: Write the route tables. Both public subnets share one table with a default route to the internet gateway. Each private subnet gets a table whose default route goes to the NAT gateway in its own AZ, so AZ b keeps working if AZ a fails. One shared NAT gateway would be cheaper, and many teams accept that for test environments.

Chain the security groups so each layer accepts traffic only from the layer in front of it. Rules name groups, not addresses, so they survive scaling. Replies need no rules, because security groups are stateful.
steps.code:
lb-sg    inbound 443    from 0.0.0.0/0     (the internet)
app-sg   inbound 8000   from lb-sg         (only the load balancer)
db-sg    inbound 5432   from app-sg        (only the app)
all three: outbound allowed, replies handled by connection tracking

steps.say: A nightly reporting job must read files from one bucket and nothing else, and `read-one-bucket.json` grants exactly that. AWS names every resource with an ARN (Amazon Resource Name), such as `arn:aws:s3:::payflow-reports`. Note the two resources: listing acts on the bucket itself, while reading acts on the objects inside it, written with `/*`. The jq summary below is easy to read, and jq fails loudly if the JSON is broken.
steps.code:
$ jq -r '.Statement[] | "\(.Effect) \(.Action) on \(.Resource)"' read-one-bucket.json
Allow s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::payflow-reports
Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::payflow-reports/*

steps.say: Last, the cost check. In this design, the load balancer and the two NAT gateways bill every hour even with no traffic, and so does any public IPv4 address. The database bills for its storage even when stopped. That list is exactly what you would delete first after a test, and on Day 35 a single `terraform destroy` removes all of it.

code.title: subnet_plan.py
code.src:
"""subnet_plan.py: check a cloud network plan before you build it.

Edit VPC and SUBNETS, then run: python3 subnet_plan.py
"""

import ipaddress
import itertools
import sys

VPC = "10.0.0.0/16"

# name: (CIDR block, availability zone, tier)
SUBNETS = {
    "public-a": ("10.0.1.0/24", "a", "public"),
    "public-b": ("10.0.2.0/24", "b", "public"),
    "private-a": ("10.0.11.0/24", "a", "private"),
    "private-b": ("10.0.12.0/24", "b", "private"),
}

# AWS keeps 5 addresses in every subnet: the first four and the last one.
AWS_RESERVED = 5


def main() -> int:
    ok = True
    vpc = ipaddress.ip_network(VPC)
    print(f"VPC {vpc}: {vpc.num_addresses} addresses")

    nets = {}
    for name, (cidr, az, tier) in SUBNETS.items():
        try:
            net = ipaddress.ip_network(cidr)
        except ValueError as err:
            print(f"BAD CIDR  {name}: {err}")
            ok = False
            continue
        nets[name] = net
        inside = net.subnet_of(vpc)
        ok = ok and inside
        usable = net.num_addresses - AWS_RESERVED
        where = "inside VPC" if inside else "OUTSIDE VPC"
        print(f"{name:10} {cidr:15} AZ {az}  {tier:8} {usable:5} usable  {where}")

    # Two subnets may never share an address.
    for (a, net_a), (b, net_b) in itertools.combinations(nets.items(), 2):
        if net_a.overlaps(net_b):
            print(f"OVERLAP   {a} {net_a} and {b} {net_b}")
            ok = False

    print("plan OK" if ok else "plan has problems")
    return 0 if ok else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Uploading is the action `s3:PutObject`, and a prefix inside a bucket is written as `arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/releases/*`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain how a request from the internet reaches an app in a private subnet, and how that app downloads a package. Mention the load balancer, security groups, route tables and the NAT gateway.
explain_back.answer: The request enters the VPC through the internet gateway and reaches the load balancer in a public subnet, whose security group allows port 443 from anywhere. The load balancer forwards it to the app in a private subnet, whose security group allows traffic only from the load balancer's group. The reply goes back automatically, because security groups are stateful. When the app downloads a package, the private subnet's route table sends that traffic to the NAT gateway in a public subnet. The NAT gateway swaps in its public address, so the app can reach out while nobody outside can connect in.

recap: The cloud rents machines, storage and services through APIs, which is why tools like Terraform can drive it.
Regions are places; availability zones are separate data centers inside them, so spread copies across AZs.
A subnet is public because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway, not because of its name.
Security groups are stateful and allow-only; NACLs are stateless, ordered and guard whole subnets.
Least privilege and short-lived role credentials beat broad permissions and long-lived keys.
Free tiers have rules that change; set a budget alert, stay in one region, and delete what you create.

check.q: Your app runs as four copies, all in two subnets of the same availability zone. That AZ loses power. What happens?
options: Traffic moves to the other subnet
Every copy goes down at once
The region moves them to a new AZ
Only half of the copies fail
check.why: Both subnets sit in the failed AZ, so every copy is lost; spreading copies across AZs is what survives this.

check.q: A subnet's NACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443 only. The app logs every request, yet clients time out. Why?
options: The security group blocks port 443
TLS cannot run inside a private subnet
Replies to ephemeral ports are dropped
The load balancer has no public IP
check.why: NACLs are stateless, so the replies, sent to the client's port between 1024 and 65535, need their own outbound rule.

check.q: A CI job must upload build files to one S3 bucket. Which setup follows least privilege and avoids long-lived keys?
options: A role allowing PutObject on that bucket, assumed via OIDC
An admin user's access key stored as a CI secret
The root account's keys with MFA turned on
A user with full S3 access and a yearly key rotation
check.why: The role grants only the one action on the one bucket, and OIDC gives the job short-lived credentials instead of a stored key.

interview.q: What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL in AWS?
interview.a: A security group attaches to a network interface, has allow rules only and is stateful, so replies to allowed traffic go through without extra rules. A network ACL applies to a whole subnet, has numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order, and is stateless, so return traffic to ephemeral ports needs explicit rules. I use security groups as the main control, chaining them by group reference, and keep NACLs for coarse subnet-wide blocks.

interview.q: Explain the shared responsibility model with an example.
interview.a: The provider secures the cloud itself: data centers, hardware, the network and the virtualization layer. The customer secures what they put in it: data, identities and permissions, network rules and configuration. On a VM service like EC2, I patch the guest operating system and configure the security group. On a serverless service like Lambda, the provider handles the runtime and OS, and I am left with my code, its permissions and its data.

interview.q: How would you keep cloud costs under control for a team?
interview.a: First visibility: tag every resource with an owner and a purpose, and send a regular cost report by tag to each team. Then guardrails: budget alerts per account, and short-lived environments built with infrastructure as code, so a test stack is destroyed with one command. Then the usual leaks: idle load balancers and NAT gateways, unattached disks and snapshots, oversized instances, and data egress. For steady workloads I would look at savings plans or reserved capacity, and spot for work that can restart.

deeper.body:
Days 10, 11 and 12 come together when you follow one request to the checkout service from the worked example, hop by hop.

1. A customer's phone asks DNS for `checkout.payflow.example`. The provider's DNS service answers with the load balancer's public addresses, one per AZ.
2. The phone opens TCP to one of them on port 443. The packet reaches the VPC through the internet gateway, and the load balancer's security group allows 443 from anywhere.
3. The load balancer runs the TLS handshake with the certificate it holds, so TLS ends here. It reads the HTTP request and picks a healthy app copy, perhaps in the other AZ.
4. It opens a new connection to the app's private address on port 8000. The app's security group allows that port only from the load balancer's group, so the packet passes.
5. The app queries the database on 5432, allowed only from the app's group, and returns a response. Every reply rides back on the same tracked connections, so no extra rules are needed.
6. Meanwhile, the app checks a fraud service on the internet. That traffic follows the private subnet's default route to the NAT gateway, which swaps in its public address.

Then ask where each failure would show up:

- A wrong DNS record: the phone never reaches you, and the error is a name or connection error, never an HTTP code.
- An expired certificate: the handshake fails in step 3, with no HTTP status at all.
- The app security group missing its rule: the load balancer cannot connect, its health checks fail, and users see 502 or 503 from the balancer.
- A slow database: the load balancer gives up waiting, and users see 504.
- A broken NAT route: checkout works until the fraud check, then that one call times out.

This mapping, from symptom to hop, is most of what an on-call engineer does in the first five minutes of an incident. Parts 12 to 16 add metrics and traces, which tell you which hop is slow without guessing.

For a real provider's version of these pieces, read AWS's [shared responsibility page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/shared-responsibility.html). Its [network ACL page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html) has a side-by-side table of security groups and NACLs.

sections.h: Open the account on the Free plan
sections.body:
Today you get a real AWS account, and the first choice comes during sign-up. Since July 15, 2025, every new account picks one of two plans:

- The Free plan gives you $100 in credits, plus up to $100 more for trying five services. It ends after six months or when the credits are used up, whichever comes first. It never charges your card.
- The Paid plan starts with the same credits, but once they are gone, you pay for what you use.

Pick the Free plan for this course. When it ends, the account closes instead of sending a bill. AWS keeps your data for 90 days after that, and upgrading in that window brings the account back.

Sign-up asks for an email address, a password, a card and a phone number for a verification code. AWS does not charge the card while you stay on the Free plan; it is there in case you upgrade later.

A few actions move a Free plan account to the Paid plan automatically, and your Free Tier credits end at once. Two of them are joining AWS Organizations and setting up an AWS Control Tower landing zone. Both are for companies that manage many accounts, and this course needs neither. Accounts opened before July 15, 2025 stay on the older 12-month free tier, which can bill you, so the budget in the next section matters even more there.

The extra $100 comes from five tasks in the Explore AWS panel on the console's home page, worth $20 each. One of them is creating a cost budget, which costs nothing, so start with that one. Some of the others, such as launching a server, spend a little of your credits.
