sections.h: Lock the root user, then set a zero-spend budget
sections.body:
The email address you signed up with is the **root user**. It can do anything in the account, including closing it, and no IAM policy can limit it. You protect it once and then put it away:

1. Turn on MFA (multi-factor authentication: a second proof on top of the password) for it. AWS now requires MFA for the root user of every account. A passkey (Touch ID on your Mac) or an authenticator app both work. You can register up to eight devices, so add a spare.
2. Never create access keys for it.
3. Create your everyday IAM user (next section), sign out, and keep root for the rare account-level task, such as changing the plan.

Then, before you create anything else, set a budget. In the console, open Billing and Cost Management, then Budgets, and pick the template called Zero spend budget. AWS describes it as a budget that notifies you once your spending exceeds the AWS Free Tier limits. Give it your email address and create it. That is also the $20 task from the Explore AWS panel.

A budget is an alarm, not a brake. As Day 12 said, it sends an email and stops nothing. Its numbers lag too: AWS refreshes budget data up to three times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after the spending. What protects you is deleting things the same day, which is why both AWS lessons end with a cleanup script. Budgets without actions cost nothing, so a second one from the Monthly cost budget template, set to $5, is a cheap extra alarm.

sections.h: People and programs get credentials in different ways
sections.body:
AWS checks every API call against credentials: an access key ID, a secret and, for temporary credentials, a session token. The CLI never sends the secret itself. It uses it to sign each request, and AWS checks the signature with its own copy of the secret. The safe rule is about where credentials come from:

- People sign in through a browser and get short-lived credentials.
- Programs, such as a server or a CI job, assume an IAM role and never hold a stored key.
- A long-lived access key is the last resort. It works for whoever holds it, copied from a laptop, a log or a git repo, until someone deletes it.

At work you will meet IAM Identity Center, AWS's single sign-on. Your company login opens a portal with every account and role you may use. You connect the CLI once with `aws configure sso`, which asks for, in order:

1. A session name of your choice.
2. The start URL of the portal, shaped like `https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start`.
3. The SSO region, then the registration scopes (keep the default).
4. Your approval in the browser window it opens.
5. The account, the role, a default region and an output format.
6. A profile name. It suggests the role and account, such as `AdministratorAccess-123456789012`.

After that, `aws sso login --profile NAME` signs you in for the day.

On your own Free plan account there is a catch. Identity Center gives access to AWS accounts only through an organization instance, which needs AWS Organizations, and that ends the Free plan. Its smaller account instance cannot give access to accounts at all.

So today you make an IAM user with a console password, MFA and the AdministratorAccess policy. It is your own sandbox, so admin rights are reasonable. Then `aws login`, in CLI 2.32.0 or later, signs the CLI in through the browser with that same login. It stores temporary credentials and refreshes them every 15 minutes, and no key ever lands on your disk. A user without admin rights needs the AWS managed policy `SignInLocalDevelopmentAccess` for it.

Programs get roles: Day 14 gives a server one through an instance profile, and Days 27 and 35 give GitHub Actions one through OIDC.

sections.h: The CLI: profiles, regions and shaping the output
sections.body:
Install the CLI with `brew install awscli`, which is version 2, and check it with `aws --version`. AWS also publishes a Mac installer package; check its install page if Homebrew is not an option. If you only have a browser, AWS CloudShell is a terminal inside the console, already signed in as you. It is free.

Settings live in named profiles in `~/.aws/config`. `aws login --profile learn` creates one called learn. Pick it for one command with `--profile learn`, or for the whole terminal with `export AWS_PROFILE=learn`.

Three habits prevent most confusion:

- Ask who you are. `aws sts get-caller-identity` prints the account and identity the CLI is using right now. STS is the Security Token Service, which hands out temporary credentials. If the ARN ends in `:root`, stop and sign in as your IAM user.
- Know your region. Each region has its own API address, such as `ec2.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com`, so each command goes to one region. It comes from `--region`, then `AWS_REGION`, then the profile. A bucket or server in another region is invisible from this one, and it still bills.
- Shape the output. The `--output` option takes json, yaml, text or table. The `--query` option takes JMESPath, a small language for picking fields out of JSON, and runs on your laptop after the answer arrives.

For example, `--query Account --output text` prints only the 12-digit number, ready for a shell variable. The jq tool from Day 5 works too, and it is better at heavy reshaping. The `--query` option needs nothing installed, so it also works in CloudShell and on servers.

Some EC2 commands accept `--dry-run`. AWS checks your permissions and the request, then refuses with `DryRunOperation` if the call would have worked. Day 14 launches its server that way first. When AWS returns an error, the CLI exits with 254, so a script with `set -e` (Day 7) stops at the failing line.

sections.h: Reading an IAM policy, and a role's two policies
sections.body:
An IAM policy is a JSON document. Open `policies/reports-reader-permissions.json` from the lab and read it next to this list:

- `Version` is always `"2012-10-17"`, the version of the policy language. You never change it.
- `Statement` is a list of rules, each with an optional `Sid`, a label for humans.
- `Effect` is Allow or Deny.
- `Action` names API calls as `service:Action`, such as `s3:GetObject`.
- `Resource` names what the call acts on, by ARN.
- `Condition` is optional and narrows the rule further.

An **ARN** has the shape `arn:aws:service:region:account:resource`. S3 bucket names are global, so bucket ARNs leave the region and account empty: `arn:aws:s3:::hello-devops-lab-123456789012`. Objects add their key, as in `.../reports/*`.

The file's first statement allows `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket, but its Condition only matches listings whose prefix starts with `reports/`. The second allows `s3:GetObject` on objects under `reports/`. Nothing allows `s3:DeleteObject`. AWS decides every call the same way: it starts from deny, a matching Allow opens the call, and an explicit Deny anywhere beats every Allow. So a delete fails.

A role carries two policies. The permissions policy, like this one, says what the role may do. The trust policy says who may assume it. In `reports-reader-trust.json` the Principal is `arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:root`, which means the whole account: any identity in it whose own policy allows `sts:AssumeRole`. It does not mean the root user.

`aws sts assume-role` checks both sides, your own policy and the role's trust policy, then hands back temporary credentials that last an hour by default. Their access key ID starts with ASIA, while long-lived keys start with AKIA, so you can tell them apart in a log.

Two AWS tools check a policy before it bites. IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation runs over 100 checks on grammar and good practice (`aws accessanalyzer validate-policy`). The policy simulator answers "would this call be allowed?" without making the call (`aws iam simulate-custom-policy`).

sections.h: S3: buckets, versions, sharing and deleting
sections.body:
S3 (Simple Storage Service) keeps files, which it calls objects, in buckets. You read and write each object whole, over HTTPS, and cannot change a few bytes in the middle as on a disk. An object's name is its key, such as `reports/2026-11-06.csv`. The slashes only look like folders. S3 has none; the console draws key prefixes as if they were.

Four rules shape what you do with it:

- Bucket names are unique across every AWS account in the world, and each name becomes part of a web address, such as `NAME.s3.amazonaws.com`. So the lab puts your account ID in the name.
- Block Public Access stops any setting from opening a bucket to the whole internet. It has four settings, and every bucket created since April 2023 starts with all four on. Leave them on. `s3-lab.sh` sets them anyway, so anyone reading the script sees the intent.
- Versioning keeps every old version of an object. Once it is on, you can suspend it but never turn it fully off. A delete then only adds a delete marker on top, and removing the marker brings the object back.
- A lifecycle rule deletes objects on a schedule. The lab's rule removes reports after 30 days, replaced versions 7 days later, and unfinished uploads after a day.

To share one private object, make a presigned URL: a link that carries a signature made with your credentials. Anyone who has the link can read that object until it expires, and from the CLI it can last up to 7 days. It also dies when the credentials that signed it expire, so a link signed with `aws login` or a role can stop working long before the time you asked for.

Deleting a versioned bucket needs one more step. The command `aws s3 rb --force` removes the current objects, but old versions and delete markers stay, and the bucket refuses to go. The lab's `cleanup.sh` deletes every version first. The few kilobytes you store today cost a tiny fraction of a cent.

sections.h: No account yet? Practise on an emulator
sections.body:
You can learn every command from today without an account. moto is a free program that pretends to be AWS on your laptop. Install it in a virtual environment, start it with `moto_server -p 5050`, and point the CLI at it: `--endpoint-url http://localhost:5050` for one command, or `export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:5050` for the whole terminal. Fake keys such as `testing` are fine. The lab README has the exact steps, and every lab script runs there.

The worked example below ran on moto, and each step says where its output differs from AWS. Some things an emulator cannot teach:

- It allows every call, so you never see AccessDenied, and the policy simulator does not run.
- New buckets have no Block Public Access until you set it, and presigned URLs never expire.
- Nothing bills, so you learn nothing about cost.
- On Day 14 no server boots and no logs arrive.

LocalStack is a bigger emulator. Since March 2026 it needs a LocalStack account and an auth token, with a free plan for non-commercial use. moto needs neither, so the course uses it.

When you go back to real AWS, unset the fake keys and the endpoint, or close that terminal tab. Left behind, they quietly win over your profile, as the common mistake below shows.

code.title: labs/aws/s3-lab.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# s3-lab.sh: Day 13's S3 steps in one go. It creates a private, versioned
# bucket, uploads a small report, shares it for 5 minutes and adds a
# lifecycle rule. Cost: a fraction of a cent. Delete it all with ./cleanup.sh.
# Usage: ./s3-lab.sh
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
source ./env.sh || exit 1

step "1. Create the bucket $LAB_BUCKET in $AWS_REGION"
if aws s3api head-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "it already exists"
else
  aws s3 mb "s3://$LAB_BUCKET"
fi
aws s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --tagging "TagSet=[{Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT}]"

step "2. Block all public access (new buckets do this already; now it is written down)"
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --query PublicAccessBlockConfiguration --output table

step "3. Turn on versioning, so an overwrite or a delete can be undone"
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --query Status --output text

step "4. Upload a small report, then list the bucket"
# "-" means: read the file's content from standard input (Day 5).
printf 'date,orders,failed\n2026-11-06,1520,12\n' | aws s3 cp - "s3://$LAB_BUCKET/reports/2026-11-06.csv"
aws s3 ls "s3://$LAB_BUCKET" --recursive --human-readable

step "5. Share the report for 5 minutes with a presigned URL"
aws s3 presign "s3://$LAB_BUCKET/reports/2026-11-06.csv" --expires-in 300

step "6. Add a lifecycle rule: delete reports after 30 days, old versions after 7"
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --lifecycle-configuration file://s3/lifecycle.json
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --query 'Rules[].{id:ID,prefix:Filter.Prefix,days:Expiration.Days,oldVersionDays:NoncurrentVersionExpiration.NoncurrentDays}' --output table

echo
echo "Done. Open the URL from step 5 in a browser, then run ./cleanup.sh when you have finished."

code.title: labs/aws/cleanup.sh (Days 13 and 14)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# cleanup.sh: delete everything Days 13 and 14 created. Safe to run again:
# it skips what is already gone and keeps going if one step fails.
# Usage: ./cleanup.sh
set -uo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")" || exit 1
source ./env.sh || exit 1

# Delete every version and delete marker in a bucket, then the bucket itself.
# "aws s3 rb --force" is not enough for a versioned bucket: old versions stay.
delete_bucket() {
  local bucket="$1" left
  if ! aws s3api head-bucket --bucket "$bucket" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "bucket $bucket: already gone"
    return 0
  fi
  while :; do
    left=$(aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket "$bucket" \
      --query 'length([Versions, DeleteMarkers][][])' --output text)
    [ "$left" = "0" ] && break
    echo "bucket $bucket: deleting $left object versions"
    aws s3api delete-objects --bucket "$bucket" --query 'length(Deleted)' --output text --delete "$(
      aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket "$bucket" --max-items 1000 --output json \
        --query '{Objects: [Versions, DeleteMarkers][][].{Key: Key, VersionId: VersionId}}'
    )" >/dev/null || return 1
  done
  aws s3 rb "s3://$bucket"
}

delete_role() {
  local role="$1" arn name
  if ! aws iam get-role --role-name "$role" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "role $role: already gone"
    return 0
  fi
  for arn in $(aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name "$role" --query 'AttachedPolicies[].PolicyArn' --output text); do
    aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name "$role" --policy-arn "$arn"
  done
  for name in $(aws iam list-role-policies --role-name "$role" --query 'PolicyNames' --output text); do
    aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name "$role" --policy-name "$name"
  done
  aws iam delete-role --role-name "$role" && echo "role $role: deleted"
}

step "1. Terminate every server tagged Project=$PROJECT (terminate deletes the disk too; stop keeps billing for it)"
ids=$(aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=tag:Project,Values=$PROJECT" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running,stopping,stopped" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text)
# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # $ids may hold several IDs, so it is split on purpose
if [ -n "$ids" ]; then
  aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids $ids --query 'TerminatingInstances[].[InstanceId,CurrentState.Name]' --output text
  echo "waiting until terminated (about a minute)"
  aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --instance-ids $ids
else
  echo "no servers with that tag"
fi

step "2. The CPU alarm, the SNS topic and the log group"
if [ "$(aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names hello-devops-cpu-high --query 'length(MetricAlarms)' --output text)" != "0" ]; then
  aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --alarm-names hello-devops-cpu-high && echo "alarm: deleted"
else
  echo "alarm: already gone"
fi
topic=$(aws sns list-topics --query "Topics[?ends_with(TopicArn, ':hello-devops-alerts')].TopicArn" --output text)
if [ -n "$topic" ]; then aws sns delete-topic --topic-arn "$topic" && echo "topic: deleted"; else echo "topic: already gone"; fi
if aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /hello-devops/app 2>/dev/null; then echo "log group: deleted"; else echo "log group: already gone"; fi

step "3. The security group (it can only go once no server uses it)"
sg=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-name,Values=hello-devops-web --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
if [ "$sg" != "None" ] && [ -n "$sg" ]; then
  for _ in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
    if aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id "$sg" 2>/dev/null; then echo "security group $sg: deleted"; break; fi
    echo "security group still in use; waiting 10 seconds"
    sleep 10
  done
else
  echo "security group: already gone"
fi

step "4. The instance profile and the IAM roles"
if aws iam get-instance-profile --instance-profile-name hello-devops-server >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  aws iam remove-role-from-instance-profile --instance-profile-name hello-devops-server --role-name hello-devops-server 2>/dev/null
  aws iam delete-instance-profile --instance-profile-name hello-devops-server && echo "instance profile: deleted"
else
  echo "instance profile: already gone"
fi
delete_role hello-devops-server
delete_role hello-devops-reports-reader

step "5. The buckets, with every old version inside them"
delete_bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
delete_bucket "$APP_BUCKET"

step "6. Anything left that could still cost money?"
echo "servers tagged Project=$PROJECT, not terminated: $(aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:Project,Values=$PROJECT" \
  "Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running,stopping,stopped" --query 'length(Reservations[].Instances[])' --output text)"
echo "Elastic IPs in $AWS_REGION: $(aws ec2 describe-addresses --query 'length(Addresses)' --output text)"
echo "unattached disks in $AWS_REGION: $(aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available --query 'length(Volumes)' --output text)"
echo "hello-devops buckets: $(aws s3api list-buckets --query "length(Buckets[?starts_with(Name, 'hello-devops-lab-') || starts_with(Name, 'hello-devops-app-')])" --output text)"
echo "All four should be 0. Check the Billing console tomorrow as well."

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how a nightly job can read one S3 folder without any stored key. Mention the trust policy, the permissions policy and temporary credentials.
explain_back.answer: The job runs with an IAM role instead of an access key. The role's trust policy says who may assume it, for example identities in my account or the EC2 service. Its permissions policy allows only `s3:ListBucket` with a `reports/` prefix and `s3:GetObject` on `reports/*`, so everything else stays denied. When the job assumes the role, STS returns temporary credentials that start with ASIA and expire after about an hour, so a copied credential is useless soon after.

recap: Pick the Free plan: when credits or six months run out, the account closes instead of billing.
Lock the root user with MFA, give it no keys, and set a zero-spend budget before anything else.
People sign in for short-lived credentials (`aws login`, or `aws configure sso` at work); programs use roles.
A policy is Effect, Action, Resource and Condition; calls start denied and any Deny wins.
A role has a trust policy (who may assume it) and a permissions policy (what it may do).
Versioned buckets keep old versions and delete markers; delete them all before the bucket.

check.q: A policy allows `s3:ListBucket` on `arn:aws:s3:::team-exports` with the condition `s3:prefix` like `2026/*`. Which command fails?
options: `aws s3 ls s3://team-exports/2026/`
`aws s3 ls s3://team-exports`
`aws s3 ls s3://team-exports/2026/11/`
None of them, because ListBucket is allowed
check.why: Listing the whole bucket sends an empty prefix, which does not match `2026/*`, so the call falls back to the default deny.

check.q: Yesterday you exported test keys for moto in this terminal. Today you run `aws login --profile learn` and `export AWS_PROFILE=learn`, and `aws s3 ls` fails with InvalidAccessKeyId. Why?
options: aws login needs a day before it works
The learn profile has no region set
The bucket list is empty on a new account
The leftover AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID beats the profile
check.why: Key variables in the environment come before the profile set by AWS_PROFILE; `aws configure list` shows their TYPE as env.

check.q: You presign a report with `--expires-in 604800` (7 days) while signed in with `aws login`. A colleague says the link already returns 403 the next morning. What is the likely cause?
options: The credentials that signed the link expired first
Presigned links never work from another network
Block Public Access turned itself off overnight
S3 deletes presigned objects after 24 hours
check.why: A presigned URL stops working when the credentials that signed it expire, even if its own expiry is later.

interview.q: How should engineers and applications get AWS credentials?
interview.a: Engineers sign in through single sign-on such as IAM Identity Center, and the CLI gets short-lived credentials from that login with `aws configure sso` and `aws sso login`. Applications use IAM roles: an instance profile on EC2, a task role on ECS, or OIDC federation for CI such as GitHub Actions. Long-lived access keys are a last resort, scoped tightly and rotated, because they work for whoever holds them until someone deletes them. The root user gets MFA, no access keys, and almost no use.

interview.q: What is the difference between a role's trust policy and its permissions policy?
interview.a: The trust policy is a resource policy on the role that names who may assume it. That can be a service like ec2.amazonaws.com, an account, or an OIDC provider with conditions on the token. The permissions policy says what the role may do once someone has assumed it. Both must allow: a principal also needs `sts:AssumeRole` in its own policy unless the trust policy names it directly. When a CI login fails with 'not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity', I look at the trust policy first.

interview.q: How do you make sure an S3 bucket never becomes public?
interview.a: I keep all four Block Public Access settings on, at the account and on each bucket, and leave ACLs disabled, which is the default for new buckets. Access goes through IAM policies on named roles, and single objects are shared with short-lived presigned URLs. A scanner in the pipeline, such as trivy on the Terraform code, fails a change that weakens those settings. IAM Access Analyzer reports any bucket that is shared outside the account.

deeper.body:
Every AWS CLI command, and every SDK such as boto3 on Day 16, looks for credentials in a fixed order and stops at the first it finds. Simplified:

1. Options on the command line, such as `--profile`.
2. Environment variables: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`.
3. The chosen profile in `~/.aws/config` and `~/.aws/credentials`: a login session, an SSO session, a role to assume, or stored keys.
4. On AWS itself, the container's or the server's role (Day 14).

`aws configure list` shows what the CLI would use and where each value came from. We tried it with test keys left in the environment and a profile called learn that held a different key. With `AWS_PROFILE=learn` exported, the access key's TYPE column said `env`: the leftover variables won. With `--profile learn` on the command line, the TYPE said `config-file`. The CLI treats a profile named on the command line as an explicit choice and skips the key variables, while `AWS_PROFILE` gets no such priority. That difference explains a lot of confusing "but I logged in" moments.

Some tools, especially older ones, do not understand `aws login` or SSO profiles yet. For them, `aws configure export-credentials --profile learn --format env` prints `export` lines with the profile's current temporary keys. Run it inside `eval "$(...)"` and that terminal has plain variables the old tool can read. They expire like any temporary credentials, so you repeat it later. Another way is a profile with a `credential_process` line, which tells a tool to run a command whenever it needs credentials.

The CLI caches temporary credentials in `~/.aws/login/cache` for `aws login` and in `~/.aws/sso/cache` for SSO. They expire, but until then they are as powerful as your login. Keep the folder private and out of container images, and remember that `aws logout` clears the login cache.

Last, the habit that ties this together: run `aws sts get-caller-identity` before anything that changes your account. It costs nothing and answers the only question that matters before a delete: which account, and as whom.

sections.h: The network your server lands in
sections.body:
Every region gives your account a default VPC, so you can launch a server before you design a network. It is the Day 12 picture, already built:

- The VPC is `172.31.0.0/16`.
- Each availability zone has one `/20` subnet: 12 free bits, so 4,096 addresses, minus the 5 that AWS keeps.
- An internet gateway is attached, and the route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to it, so every default subnet is public.
- A server launched there gets a public IPv4 address unless you ask it not to.

The server itself still sees only its private address, such as `172.31.0.5`. The internet gateway translates between the two (Day 12).

That is enough for one learning server. Production teams build their own VPC, with private subnets for apps and databases, as you sketched on Day 12.

The firewall is a security group. It is stateful (Day 12), so replies to allowed traffic go out without a rule of their own. Its outbound rules allow everything by default, which lets the server download packages. `server-up.sh` makes a group called `hello-devops-web` with no inbound rules at all. Nobody on the internet can start a connection to the server, you included. That sounds like a problem until the next section.

sections.h: A shell without opening port 22
sections.body:
On Day 7 you logged in to a machine with SSH, which needs port 22 open and a key. AWS gives you three ways in, and the one to use needs neither.

Session Manager, part of AWS Systems Manager, works the other way round. A small program on the server, the SSM Agent (SSM is Systems Manager's old short name), keeps an outbound HTTPS connection open to Systems Manager. The security group is stateful, so traffic on that connection flows both ways with no inbound rule. When you run `aws ssm start-session --target i-...`, AWS checks your IAM permissions and joins your terminal to that connection. It needs four things:

1. The SSM Agent on the server. AWS's and Canonical's Ubuntu images, and Amazon Linux 2023, come with it.
2. An instance role with the AWS managed policy `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`.
3. Outbound HTTPS from the server to three endpoints in its region: `ssm`, `ssmmessages` and `ec2messages`. A public IP and the default outbound rule cover it.
4. The Session Manager plugin for the CLI on your Mac: `brew install --cask session-manager-plugin`.

It costs nothing extra on EC2, and there is no port to open and no key to lose. You arrive as `ssm-user`, a user the agent creates, with sudo rights. It forwards ports too: the document `AWS-StartPortForwardingSession` makes `localhost:8000` on your Mac reach port 8000 on the server.

EC2 Instance Connect is the second way. It pushes a one-time SSH key for you, but port 22 must still be open, either to AWS's Instance Connect address range or through an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint.

Key pairs are the old way: AWS keeps the public key, you download a private `.pem` file once, and you open port 22. That is Day 7's SSH plus a file you must never lose or leak.

sections.h: Choosing the machine: image, type and price
sections.body:
An **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image) is the disk image a server starts from. AMI IDs differ per region and change with every update, so look them up by name instead of copying one. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, publishes the newest Ubuntu IDs as public parameters in Parameter Store, a store of named values in Systems Manager, and `server-up.sh` reads `/aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/24.04/stable/current/arm64/hvm/ebs-gp3/ami-id`.

The lab runs Ubuntu 24.04 because you know it from the Part 1 practice container. Its Python 3.12 is also new enough for gunicorn 26, which needs 3.10 or later. Amazon Linux 2023, AWS's own system, is a fine choice too. Its built-in `python3`, though, stays at 3.9 for the whole life of the release, so you would install a newer one first.

The instance type sets CPU and memory. The lab uses `t4g.micro`: 2 vCPUs (virtual CPUs), 1 GiB of memory and a Graviton processor. Graviton is ARM, like your Mac's chip, which is why the image is arm64. The Free plan lists six eligible types: t3.micro, t3.small, t4g.micro, t4g.small, c7i-flex.large and m7i-flex.large.

T types are burstable, made for servers that are mostly idle and sometimes busy. Each has a baseline, the share of CPU it may use all day: 10% per vCPU for `t4g.micro`. Below the baseline it saves up CPU credits, and above it the server spends them. In the default unlimited mode, staying above the baseline over a day costs extra. The script launches in standard mode, where the server slows down instead.

In us-east-1, checked today:

- The instance costs $0.0084 an hour.
- Its public IPv4 address costs $0.005 an hour, the same as an Elastic IP, used or not.
- Its 8 GB gp3 disk costs $0.08 per GB-month, about 64 cents a month.

A two-hour session comes to about 3 cents, paid from Free plan credits.

Stop and terminate are different. A stopped server ends the compute bill, keeps its disk and that disk's bill, and gives back its public IP, so it gets a new one on start. Terminating deletes the server and, by default, its disk.

sections.h: User data: a server that installs itself
sections.body:
User data is a script you hand to EC2 at launch. On the first boot, a tool called cloud-init fetches it from the instance metadata service (see below) and runs it once, as root. It may be up to 16 KB, and everything it prints lands in `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log` on the server, which is where you look first when something is missing.

The lab's `server/user-data.sh` turns a bare Ubuntu server into a hello-devops server in seven steps:

1. Install `python3-venv`, `unzip` and `curl` with apt.
2. Install the AWS CLI v2 from AWS's official zip, unless the image already has it.
3. Create a system user `hello` that cannot log in.
4. Copy the app files from S3 with `aws s3 cp`, using the server's role.
5. Make a virtual environment and `pip install` the requirements.
6. Install `hello-devops.service`, then `systemctl enable --now` it.
7. Install the CloudWatch agent and load its config.

It is Day 7's bash with `set -euo pipefail`, so a failed step stops the script. One line handles a cloud quirk: Ubuntu may update itself during its first boot, so apt waits up to five minutes for its lock instead of failing.

Why systemd, and not `nohup gunicorn &`? Day 6 already answered it. The service manager starts the app at boot, restarts it after a crash (`Restart=on-failure`), runs it as `hello` instead of root, and sends its output to the journal. The unit binds gunicorn to `0.0.0.0:8000` so outside traffic can reach it (Day 10), and leaves the security group to decide who may.

Installing on every new server is slow, two to four minutes here. Teams that launch many servers bake the result into their own AMI, or ship the app as a container image (Part 5). Days 36 and 37 show Ansible, which configures servers that are already running.

sections.h: A role on the server instead of keys
sections.body:
The server reads S3 and writes to CloudWatch, so it needs credentials. Copying your access key onto it would put a long-lived key on a machine the internet can reach. A role does the job without one.

EC2 attaches a role through an instance profile, a wrapper that holds exactly one role. Software on the server asks the instance metadata service (IMDS) for the role's temporary credentials, and the AWS CLI does that by itself. IMDS lives at `169.254.169.254`, an address only the server itself can reach. The credentials rotate automatically, and you never manage a file of keys.

`server-up.sh` launches with `HttpTokens=required`, which means IMDSv2 only: a program must first fetch a session token with a PUT request before IMDS answers anything. A web app that an attacker tricks into fetching a URL has a much harder time stealing the credentials that way. Such tricks usually send a plain GET, and cannot send a PUT with a special header first.

The role `hello-devops-server` carries three policies:

- `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`, AWS's managed policy for Session Manager.
- `CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy`, AWS's managed policy for the agent.
- `read-app-files`, our own: list and read `app/` in one bucket, and nothing else.

A new role takes a few seconds to reach EC2. Launch too soon and EC2 calls the instance profile invalid, so the script waits and retries.

sections.h: CloudWatch: metrics, an alarm and the app's logs
sections.body:
CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service, and an EC2 server reports to it from its first minute. Basic monitoring is on and free: CPU, network and disk activity every 5 minutes, plus status checks, AWS's own tests that the server and its hardware respond. Memory and free disk space are missing, because AWS cannot see inside your operating system; the CloudWatch agent can add them.

An alarm watches one metric and is in one of three states: OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which is where a new alarm starts. The script `alarm.sh` makes one that goes to ALARM when the average CPU stays above 70% for two 5-minute periods in a row. Needing two in a row means one short spike sends no email. On every change of state it sends a message to an SNS (Simple Notification Service) topic, a named mailbox that delivers to your email. SNS first sends a confirmation email, and nothing arrives until you click its link. To test the chain without loading the server, `aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state` flips the alarm to ALARM by hand. The first 10 alarms are in the free tier.

For logs you have two choices:

- The simple one: open a session and run `journalctl -u hello-devops -f`. For one server you check now and then, that is enough.
- The CloudWatch agent: it reads the journal and sends the `hello-devops` unit's lines to the log group `/hello-devops/app`, one stream per server. The agent learned to read journald in 2026; before that, people installed rsyslog to write log files for it.

The agent earns its place when servers come and go. Logs outlive a terminated server, and `aws logs tail /hello-devops/app --follow` shows every server at once. The free tier covers 5 GB of logs a month, far more than this lab writes. Parts 12 to 14 go much further with Prometheus, Grafana and the Elastic stack.

sections.h: One script for the launch, then a console tour
sections.body:
The script `server-up.sh` prints a heading for each of its six steps. The order matters, because the launch in step 6 uses everything the first five made:

1. Upload the app files to S3.
2. Create the role and the instance profile.
3. Create the security group.
4. Look up the AMI.
5. Fill in user data.
6. Launch.

The launch first runs with `--dry-run`. Only when AWS answers DryRunOperation does the script launch for real and wait until the server runs. Every piece carries the tag `Project=hello-devops`, the same tag Day 35's Terraform and Day 37's Ansible inventory use, and `cleanup.sh` uses it to find the server. The server also gets `Role=web` and an `owner` tag with your user name.

Then look at the same things in the console, in the same region:

1. EC2, then Instances: the state, the public IP, and the Connect button, whose Session Manager tab opens a shell in the browser.
2. EC2, then Security Groups: the inbound rules of `hello-devops-web`, empty until you add one.
3. CloudWatch: Alarms, then Log groups.
4. Billing and Cost Management, then Bills, the next day, to see the cents by service.

From here, Day 35 moves AWS work into Terraform, where one destroy removes it all. Days 36 and 37 configure servers like this one with Ansible, and Part 10 meets EKS, AWS's managed Kubernetes.

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
# user-data.sh: cloud-init runs this once, as root, when the server first boots
# (Day 14). It installs hello-devops and runs it as a systemd service.
# server-up.sh fills in the two values below before it launches the server.
# Read what happened on the server with: sudo cat /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
set -euo pipefail

BUCKET="__BUCKET__" # the bucket server-up.sh uploaded the app files to
REGION="__REGION__" # the region this server runs in

export AWS_REGION="$REGION"
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive # apt must never stop and ask a question
# On first boot Ubuntu may be updating itself; wait for apt's lock, do not fail.
APT="apt-get -y -q -o DPkg::Lock::Timeout=300"

echo "== 1. Packages: Python's venv module, unzip and curl"
$APT update
$APT install python3-venv unzip curl

echo "== 2. The AWS CLI v2, from the official zip (aarch64 on Graviton)"
if ! command -v aws >/dev/null; then
  curl -fsSL "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-$(uname -m).zip" -o /tmp/awscliv2.zip
  unzip -q /tmp/awscliv2.zip -d /tmp
  /tmp/aws/install
  rm -rf /tmp/aws /tmp/awscliv2.zip
fi

echo "== 3. A system user for the app, with no login shell"
id hello >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd --system --home-dir /opt/hello-devops --shell /usr/sbin/nologin hello

echo "== 4. The app files from S3, read with the instance role (no keys here)"
mkdir -p /opt/hello-devops
aws s3 cp "s3://$BUCKET/app/" /opt/hello-devops/ --recursive --no-progress

echo "== 5. A virtual environment with the app's dependencies"
python3 -m venv /opt/hello-devops/venv
/opt/hello-devops/venv/bin/pip install --quiet --disable-pip-version-check -r /opt/hello-devops/requirements.txt
chown -R hello:hello /opt/hello-devops

echo "== 6. Run the app as a systemd service (Day 6)"
install -m 644 /opt/hello-devops/hello-devops.service /etc/systemd/system/hello-devops.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now hello-devops

echo "== 7. The CloudWatch agent: it sends the app's journal to CloudWatch Logs"
curl -fsSL "https://amazoncloudwatch-agent.s3.amazonaws.com/ubuntu/$(dpkg --print-architecture)/latest/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.deb" -o /tmp/cwagent.deb
dpkg -i -E /tmp/cwagent.deb
rm -f /tmp/cwagent.deb
/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \
  -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/hello-devops/cloudwatch-agent.json

echo "== Done: hello-devops listens on port 8000"

# hello-devops.service: run the app with gunicorn under systemd (Day 14).
# user-data.sh copies this file to /etc/systemd/system/ and starts it.
[Unit]
Description=hello-devops web app
# gunicorn binds a port, so start once the network is up.
After=network-online.target

User=hello
Group=hello
WorkingDirectory=/opt/hello-devops
Environment=APP_VERSION=1.0.0
Environment="GREETING=Hello from EC2"
# Print log lines at once, so journalctl and CloudWatch see them immediately.
Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# line per request to the journal.

# Start it again if it crashes, but not after a clean stop (Day 6).
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2

WantedBy=multi-user.target

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# server-up.sh: Day 14. Launch one small Ubuntu server that runs hello-devops.
# It creates, all tagged Project=hello-devops:
#   - an S3 bucket with the app files (app.py, requirements.txt, the unit file)
#   - an IAM role and instance profile, so the server needs no keys
#   - a security group with no inbound rules
#   - one t4g.micro instance (ARM, Graviton) with a public IPv4 address
# Cost while it runs: about 1.5 US cents an hour in us-east-1 (README).
# Delete everything with ./cleanup.sh.
# Usage: ./server-up.sh    (APP_DIR defaults to ~/code/hello-devops)
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
source ./env.sh || exit 1

APP_DIR="${APP_DIR:-$HOME/code/hello-devops}"
INSTANCE_TYPE="${INSTANCE_TYPE:-t4g.micro}"
ROLE=hello-devops-server
SG_NAME=hello-devops-web
AMI_PARAM=/aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/24.04/stable/current/arm64/hvm/ebs-gp3/ami-id

running=$(aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=tag:Project,Values=$PROJECT" "Name=tag:Name,Values=hello-devops" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running,stopping,stopped" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text)
if [ -n "$running" ]; then
  echo "A lab server already exists: $running. Run ./cleanup.sh first if you want a new one."
  exit 0
fi

step "1. Upload the app files to s3://$APP_BUCKET/app/"
[ -f "$APP_DIR/app.py" ] || { echo "No app.py in $APP_DIR. Set APP_DIR to your hello-devops folder." >&2; exit 1; }
if ! aws s3api head-bucket --bucket "$APP_BUCKET" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  aws s3 mb "s3://$APP_BUCKET"
fi
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "$APP_BUCKET" \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket "$APP_BUCKET" --tagging "TagSet=[{Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT}]"
for f in "$APP_DIR/app.py" "$APP_DIR/requirements.txt" server/hello-devops.service server/cloudwatch-agent.json; do
  aws s3 cp "$f" "s3://$APP_BUCKET/app/" --no-progress
done

step "2. An IAM role for the server, so no keys ever live on it"
if ! aws iam get-role --role-name "$ROLE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  aws iam create-role --role-name "$ROLE" --assume-role-policy-document file://policies/ec2-trust.json \
    --tags "Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT" --query Role.Arn --output text
fi
# Two AWS managed policies: Session Manager, and the CloudWatch agent.
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy
# Our own small policy: read the app/ folder of one bucket, nothing else.
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE" --policy-name read-app-files \
  --policy-document "$(sed "s/ACCOUNT_ID/$ACCOUNT_ID/g" policies/hello-server-permissions.json)"
# EC2 attaches a role through an instance profile, a small wrapper around it.
if ! aws iam get-instance-profile --instance-profile-name "$ROLE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name "$ROLE" --tags "Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT" \
    --query InstanceProfile.Arn --output text
  aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name "$ROLE" --role-name "$ROLE"
fi

step "3. A security group in the default VPC, with no inbound rules at all"
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=is-default,Values=true --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)
[ "$VPC_ID" != "None" ] || { echo "This region has no default VPC. See the README." >&2; exit 1; }
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters "Name=group-name,Values=$SG_NAME" "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID" \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
if [ "$SG_ID" = "None" ]; then
  SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name "$SG_NAME" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" \
    --description "hello-devops lab server (Day 14)" \
    --tag-specifications "ResourceType=security-group,Tags=[{Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT}]" \
    --query GroupId --output text)
fi
echo "$SG_ID in $VPC_ID"
# Not every availability zone offers every instance type, so pick one that does.
AZ=$(aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings --location-type availability-zone \
  --filters "Name=instance-type,Values=$INSTANCE_TYPE" --query 'sort(InstanceTypeOfferings[].Location)[0]' --output text)
SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID" "Name=availability-zone,Values=$AZ" \
  "Name=default-for-az,Values=true" --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --output text)
echo "$INSTANCE_TYPE in $AZ, public subnet $SUBNET_ID"

step "4. The newest Ubuntu 24.04 image for ARM, from Canonical's public parameter"
AMI_ID="${AMI_ID:-$(aws ssm get-parameter --name "$AMI_PARAM" --query Parameter.Value --output text)}"
echo "$AMI_ID"

step "5. Fill in user-data.sh with the bucket and the region"
user_data=$(mktemp)
sed -e "s/__BUCKET__/$APP_BUCKET/" -e "s/__REGION__/$AWS_REGION/" server/user-data.sh >"$user_data"

launch() {
  aws ec2 run-instances "$@" --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type "$INSTANCE_TYPE" \
    --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --iam-instance-profile "Name=$ROLE" \
    --user-data "file://$user_data" \
    --credit-specification CpuCredits=standard \
    --metadata-options HttpTokens=required \
    --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=hello-devops},{Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT},{Key=Role,Value=web},{Key=owner,Value=$OWNER}]" \
    --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text
}

# A new role takes a few seconds to reach EC2. Until then EC2 calls the
# instance profile invalid, so wait and try again.
launch_with_retry() {
  local out attempt
  for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
    if out=$(launch "$@" 2>&1); then
      echo "$out"
      return 0
    fi
    if echo "$out" | grep -q DryRunOperation; then
      echo "dry run: the request would succeed" >&2
      return 0
    fi
    if echo "$out" | grep -qi "instance profile" && [ "$attempt" -lt 8 ]; then
      echo "the new role has not reached EC2 yet; waiting 10 seconds" >&2
      sleep 10
    else
      echo "$out" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

step "6. Ask AWS whether the launch would work (--dry-run), then launch"
launch_with_retry --dry-run
INSTANCE_ID=$(launch_with_retry)
rm -f "$user_data"
echo "launched $INSTANCE_ID; waiting until it is running"
aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID"
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].{id:InstanceId,type:InstanceType,az:Placement.AvailabilityZone,publicIp:PublicIpAddress,privateIp:PrivateIpAddress}' \
  --output table

cat <<EOF

The server is booting and user-data.sh is installing the app (2 to 4 minutes).
Next steps (Day 14):
  aws ssm start-session --target $INSTANCE_ID
  aws ssm start-session --target $INSTANCE_ID --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession --parameters '{"portNumber":["8000"],"localPortNumber":["8000"]}'
When you are finished: ./cleanup.sh
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# alarm.sh: Day 14. Email you when the lab server's CPU stays above 70%
# for two 5-minute periods in a row. Uses the free basic EC2 metrics.
# Usage: ./alarm.sh you@example.com
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
EMAIL="${1:?Usage: ./alarm.sh you@example.com}"
source ./env.sh || exit 1

INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=tag:Project,Values=$PROJECT" "Name=tag:Name,Values=hello-devops" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
[ -n "$INSTANCE_ID" ] && [ "$INSTANCE_ID" != "None" ] || { echo "No running lab server. Run ./server-up.sh first." >&2; exit 1; }

step "1. An SNS topic: one address that alarms send messages to"
TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic --name hello-devops-alerts --tags "Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT" \
  --query TopicArn --output text)
echo "$TOPIC_ARN"

step "2. Subscribe your email. AWS sends a confirmation email: click its link"
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn "$TOPIC_ARN" --protocol email --notification-endpoint "$EMAIL" \
  --query SubscriptionArn --output text

step "3. The alarm: average CPUUtilization above 70% for 2 periods of 5 minutes"
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name hello-devops-cpu-high \
  --alarm-description "CPU above 70% for 10 minutes on the hello-devops lab server" \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --dimensions "Name=InstanceId,Value=$INSTANCE_ID" \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 2 --threshold 70 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching \
  --alarm-actions "$TOPIC_ARN" --ok-actions "$TOPIC_ARN" --tags "Key=Project,Value=$PROJECT"
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names hello-devops-cpu-high \
  --query 'MetricAlarms[0].{alarm:AlarmName,state:StateValue,threshold:Threshold}' --output table

cat <<EOF

Test the email path without waiting for real load:
  aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name hello-devops-cpu-high --state-value ALARM --state-reason "Testing by hand"
EOF

lessons.mistake: Stopping the server and calling it cleaned up. A stopped instance ends only the compute bill: its disk keeps billing, and so does any Elastic IP you allocated. Terminate it, then run `./cleanup.sh` and check that its last four lines all end in 0.
lessons.real_world: In a team that runs a payments API on EC2, no security group anywhere allows port 22. Engineers open Session Manager sessions through their single sign-on role, and the sessions are logged to S3 for auditors. New servers start from a baked AMI with the app already installed. An Auto Scaling group, a rule that keeps a set number of servers running, replaces a failing one without anyone logging in.

task.title: Your server, open to you alone, then gone
steps: No account? Run `server-up.sh`, `alarm.sh` and `cleanup.sh` against moto as the lab README shows, then read the remaining steps instead of doing them.
Install the Session Manager plugin, sign in with `aws login --profile learn`, and run `./server-up.sh` from `~/code/aws-lab`. Note the instance ID.
Open a shell with `aws ssm start-session`. Wait for `cloud-init status --wait`, read the end of the user data log, and check the service with `systemctl status` and `journalctl`.
Still on the server, run `whoami` and `aws sts get-caller-identity`. Explain both answers: who you are in Linux, and which identity the server's CLI uses.
In a second terminal on your Mac, start port forwarding to port 8000 and `curl localhost:8000` a few times.
From your Mac, `curl` the server's public IP on port 8000 with `--max-time 5`. Name the failure, using Day 10's list of errors.
Add a security group rule for port 8000 from your own IP as a `/32`, curl the public IP again, then revoke the rule.
Run `./alarm.sh` with your email, confirm the subscription, force the alarm to ALARM, and wait for the email.
Run `aws logs tail /hello-devops/app --follow` and make a few requests through the port forward until their log lines appear.
Run `./cleanup.sh`, check the last four counts, and look at Bills by service in the console tomorrow.
hints: If start-session says the target is not connected, wait a minute: the agent registers after boot, and only once the role has reached the server.
A curl that hangs until the timeout means the packets are dropped; a refused connection means they arrived and nothing listened.
Your home IP from checkip.amazonaws.com can change when your router reconnects, and then the /32 rule no longer matches.
task.done_when: You are done when the public IP answers on port 8000 only while your /32 rule exists, the alarm email arrived, and ./cleanup.sh ends with four zeros.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how your server installed and started the app with nobody logged in, and how it read S3 without a key. Mention user data, systemd and the instance profile.
explain_back.answer: At launch I passed `user-data.sh` as user data, and cloud-init ran it once as root on the first boot. The script installed Python and the AWS CLI, copied the app from S3 and built a virtual environment. Then it installed a systemd unit that runs gunicorn as the `hello` user and restarts it after a crash. The S3 copy worked because the instance profile attaches the `hello-devops-server` role, and the CLI fetched that role's temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. No key was ever written to the server, and the role can only read the `app/` folder of one bucket.

recap: The default VPC has one public subnet per zone; a security group with no inbound rules blocks every new connection.
Session Manager gives you a shell through an outbound agent: no port 22, no key, just IAM.
Look up AMIs by public parameter; t4g.micro is ARM, cheap and on the Free plan list.
User data runs once at first boot as root; systemd keeps the app running after that.
An instance profile gives the server a role, so it never holds a stored key.
Stop keeps the disk and its bill; terminate ends both, and cleanup.sh checks for leftovers.

check.q: A teammate's security group allows port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 so they can SSH in. Which change gives them a shell and closes the port?
options: Allow port 22 only from 10.0.0.0/8 instead
Move the key pair file into the repository
Use Session Manager and delete the port 22 rule
Swap the security group for a network ACL
check.why: Session Manager needs no inbound port at all; the agent connects out, and IAM decides who may open a session.

check.q: Your new server answers nothing on port 8000, and `systemctl status hello-devops` says the unit does not exist. Where do you look first?
options: /var/log/cloud-init-output.log on the server
The CloudWatch CPU graph for the instance
The security group's outbound rules
The budget alerts in the Billing console
check.why: The unit is installed by user data, and everything user data printed, including the line where it stopped, is in that log.

check.q: An alarm has a 300-second period, 2 evaluation periods and a threshold of 70. CPU averages 90% for one 5-minute period, then 5% for the next. What happens?
options: It goes to ALARM after the first period
It stays OK, because two periods in a row must breach
It goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA after the spike
It goes to ALARM after the second period
check.why: With 2 evaluation periods, the alarm needs two breaching 5-minute averages in a row, and the second one was 5%.

interview.q: How do you give an application on EC2 access to S3?
interview.a: I create an IAM role whose trust policy allows the EC2 service, and give it a policy for exactly the buckets and prefixes it needs. Then I attach it through an instance profile. The SDK or CLI on the server picks up temporary credentials from the instance metadata service and refreshes them by itself. I launch with IMDSv2 required, so a server-side request forgery bug cannot read the credentials easily. I never copy access keys onto a server.

interview.q: How do you get a shell on a server that has no SSH port open?
interview.a: With Systems Manager Session Manager. The SSM Agent on the server keeps an outbound HTTPS connection to Systems Manager, and `aws ssm start-session` joins my terminal to it after an IAM check. It needs the agent, an instance role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, outbound HTTPS to the ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages endpoints, and the plugin on my laptop. Sessions can be logged, and port forwarding replaces most SSH tunnels.

interview.q: What is the difference between stopping and terminating an EC2 instance, and what keeps costing money?
interview.a: Stopping shuts the server down but keeps it and its EBS volumes, so I can start it again later. The compute bill stops, the disk bill does not, and an auto-assigned public IP is released. Terminating deletes the instance and, by default, its root volume. Things that bill while idle include volumes and snapshots, Elastic IPs, NAT gateways and load balancers. For lab work I terminate and delete everything the same day, and I check the bill by service the next morning.

deeper.body:
Three things happen on the server before your app answers, and you can watch each one from a Session Manager shell.

First, the metadata service. Ask it for a token, then use the token:

1. `TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300")` asks for a token that lasts five minutes.
2. `curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` prints the role's name, `hello-devops-server`.
3. Add that name to the end of the URL, and you see the temporary credentials themselves, with their expiry time.

Without the token header the request is refused, because the server allows IMDSv2 only. On the server, `aws sts get-caller-identity` prints an assumed-role ARN whose last part is the instance ID, which is how AWS names the role session for a server.

Second, cloud-init. It works through stages during boot, and your user data runs in the last one, after the network is up. It keeps a copy of the script under `/var/lib/cloud/instances/` in a folder named after the instance ID, and `cloud-init status --long` reports whether it finished and what failed. Because user data runs on the first boot only, editing it on a stopped server changes nothing. Launch a new server instead: Terraform, Auto Scaling groups and Kubernetes all build on that habit of replacing servers rather than repairing them.

Third, the choice between baking and bootstrapping. Our user data downloads and installs everything on every new server, which takes minutes and depends on apt, PyPI and AWS's download site being up at that moment. Baking moves that work earlier: a tool such as HashiCorp's Packer starts a temporary server, runs the same install steps, and saves the disk as your own AMI. New servers then boot ready, and user data only sets what differs per server, such as a version or a greeting. Containers push the same idea further: the image you build in Part 5 is a baked app that runs anywhere.

For one lab server, bootstrapping with user data is the right call. For a fleet that must replace servers quickly, bake the slow parts and keep user data small.

recap: An IP address finds the machine and a port finds the program; private addresses reach the internet through NAT.
/N fixes N bits: /24 holds 256 addresses and /16 holds 65,536; apps in containers bind to 0.0.0.0.
DNS walks from your resolver to root, TLD and authoritative servers, and caches each answer for its TTL.
Unresolved means DNS, refused means no listener, and a timeout means a drop or a wrong address.
HTTP is text with methods, headers and status codes; TLS encrypts it and proves the server's name.
A reverse proxy ends TLS and balances load, and 502, 503 and 504 usually come from it.
In the cloud, route tables make subnets public or private; security groups are stateful and NACLs are not.
On AWS: Free plan, root MFA and a zero-spend budget first; people get short-lived logins and programs get roles.
An IAM policy is Effect, Action, Resource and Condition; calls start denied, and any Deny wins.
A server should install itself with user data and systemd, be reached through Session Manager, and be terminated when done.

flashcards.front: What does /24 mean, and how many addresses does it hold?
flashcards.back: The first 24 bits are fixed; the block holds 256 addresses.

flashcards.front: Name the three private IPv4 ranges.
What does NAT do in your home router?
flashcards.back: It swaps your private source address for its public one on the way out, remembers the swap, and reverses it for replies.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and to 0.0.0.0?
flashcards.back: 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections; 0.0.0.0 listens on every address the machine has.

flashcards.front: Connection refused or timed out: what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Refused: the host answered but nothing listens on the port. Timed out: no answer, usually a firewall drop or a wrong address.

flashcards.front: In what order does a DNS lookup travel when nothing is cached?
flashcards.back: Stub resolver, recursive resolver, root server, TLD server, authoritative server.
401: who are you? (no or bad credentials). 403: I know you, and you may not do this.
502: the proxy got no good answer from the app. 504: the proxy waited for the app and gave up.

flashcards.front: Layer 4 or layer 7 load balancer?
flashcards.back: L4 forwards connections by address and port. L7 reads HTTP and can route by host, path and headers.

flashcards.front: Security group or network ACL?
flashcards.back: Security group: stateful, allow-only, on a network interface. NACL: stateless, ordered allow and deny, on a subnet.

flashcards.front: Does an AWS budget alert stop your spending?
flashcards.back: No. It only sends a notification, and its data can lag by hours; the resources keep running.

flashcards.front: What happens when a Free plan account's credits or six months run out?
flashcards.back: The account closes instead of charging you. AWS keeps your data for 90 days, and upgrading in that window brings it back.

flashcards.front: Which identity should never have access keys?
flashcards.back: The root user. Protect it with MFA and use it only for account-level tasks.

flashcards.front: How is `aws login` safer than an access key in ~/.aws/credentials?
flashcards.back: It turns your console sign-in into temporary credentials that the CLI refreshes; a stored key works until someone deletes it.

flashcards.front: In a trust policy, what does `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root` mean?
flashcards.back: The whole account: any identity in it whose own policy allows sts:AssumeRole. It does not mean the root user.

flashcards.front: An access key ID starts with ASIA. What does that tell you?
flashcards.back: It is temporary, from a role or a session. Long-lived keys start with AKIA.

flashcards.front: Why does `aws s3 rb --force` fail on a versioned bucket?
flashcards.back: It deletes only the current objects; old versions and delete markers remain. Delete every version first.

flashcards.front: What four things does Session Manager need?
flashcards.back: The SSM Agent, an instance role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, outbound HTTPS to the SSM endpoints, and the plugin on your laptop.

flashcards.front: Where do you look when EC2 user data seems to have done nothing?
flashcards.back: In /var/log/cloud-init-output.log on the server.

flashcards.front: Stop or terminate: which one ends the disk bill?
flashcards.back: Terminate. A stopped instance keeps its EBS disk, and the disk keeps billing.

quiz.q: An app in a container listens on 127.0.0.1:8000. You run it with `-p 8000:8000` and curl localhost:8000 on your Mac. What happens?
options: It works, because Docker forwards the port
Docker refuses to start the container
curl gets an empty reply or a reset
It works, but only over HTTPS
quiz.why: Docker forwards to the container's network address, and an app bound to the container's loopback never sees that traffic.
32 minus 22 leaves 10 free bits, and 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024.

quiz.q: You changed an A record whose TTL is 3600. Twenty minutes later, some users still reach the old server. Why?
options: The new server's firewall blocks them
Their browsers do not support TLS
The registrar has not approved it yet
Caches keep the old answer for the TTL
quiz.why: Resolvers may reuse a cached answer until its TTL of one hour runs out.

quiz.q: `aws sts get-caller-identity` prints an ARN that ends in `:root` on your learning account. What should you do?
options: Carry on, because root is fine for a lab
Create an access key for root and use that
Sign out, sign in as your IAM user, run aws login again
Turn off MFA so the CLI can refresh the session
quiz.why: The root user can do anything and no policy limits it; daily work, including the CLI, belongs to your IAM user with MFA.

quiz.q: Your load balancer returns 502 Bad Gateway for every request. Where do you look first?
options: The client's browser settings
Whether the app behind it is up
The domain's DNS records
The certificate's expiry date
quiz.why: 502 means the proxy itself works but could not get a good answer from the app behind it.

quiz.q: What makes an AWS subnet public?
options: Its name contains the word public
It has a route to a NAT gateway
Its CIDR block is exactly a /24
A 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway
quiz.why: The route table decides: a default route to an internet gateway makes the subnet reachable from the internet.

quiz.q: Your server's security group has no inbound rules. From your Mac, `curl --max-time 5 http://PUBLIC_IP:8000` waits and then times out. What does that tell you?
options: The app on the server has crashed
DNS cannot resolve the address
The server ran out of CPU credits
The security group drops the packets
quiz.why: A security group silently drops traffic it does not allow, so the client times out; a crashed app behind an open port would answer with connection refused.

quiz.q: Versioning is on, and you ran `aws s3 rm` on a report by mistake. How do you get it back?
options: Delete the delete marker on top of it
Wait for the lifecycle rule to restore it
You cannot; S3 deletes are permanent
Run aws s3 rb --force on the bucket
quiz.why: In a versioned bucket a delete only adds a delete marker; removing the marker makes the newest version current again.

quiz.q: In access.log, field 9 is the status code. Which pipeline counts how many responses had each status code?
options: `grep 9 access.log | wc -l`
`sort access.log | uniq -c | awk '{print $9}' | head`
`awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c`
`cut -f9 access.log | uniq`
quiz.why: awk picks the status field, sort puts equal codes together, and `uniq -c` counts each group; uniq only merges neighbouring lines.

quiz.q: In the practice box you run `apt install dnsutils` to get dig, exit, and start a new box. dig is missing again. Why?
options: `--rm` deleted the old container
dig only works in a Multipass VM
apt removes packages after an hour
Docker Desktop resets the image daily
quiz.why: Every docker run starts fresh from the image, and `--rm` threw away the container where you installed dig.
